Mr. Erickson was vaulted by the Prime Minister over the four finalists recommended by the selection committee. I therefore move, seconded by the hon. member for Moose Jaw (Mr. Neil):
That this represents pork-barrel politics of the worst kind and makes a complete mockery of the tender and competition process, and that the decision be returned to cabinet for honest review and the ed 177;-1 eventual appointment of one of the four candidates recommended by the selection committee.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise to move a motion under the provisions of Standing Order 43. While the federal government evades action by conducting studies and holding conferences, hundreds of thousands of Canadian women are struggling to survive on low wages, without adequate training programs, decent day care, or equal pay for work of equal value. Many have been laid off and thousands more face permanent unemployment due to technological change. Therefore I move, seconded by the hon. member for Churchill (Mr. Murphy):
That the federal government and the minister responsible for the status of women set a positive example for the provinces by establishing adequate pension plans for women, providing start up funds for universal day care, implementing mandatory affirmative action, and expanding pre-employment and high tech training programs for women, with allowances to cover child care.

subsubtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT-QUERY RESPECTING GOVERNMENT POLICIES
speechtext:
Before I ask my question, Madam Speaker, I am sure the Chair and the House would want me to extend on behalf of the House our condolences to the Right Hon. Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark), whose father passed away last night.
Oral Questions
My question is directed to the Right Hon. Prime Minister. He is aware from the figures published last Friday that unemployment in the country now stands at the highest level since the depression. Yesterday the Minister of Finance said in Paris that unemployment is unlikely to rise further and that there was a new urgency for efforts to promote what he called sustainable recovery. What new policies is the Prime Minister or his government bringing forward in order that we have the recovery about which the Minister of Finance spoke in Paris, without throwing more hundreds and hundreds of people out of work?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
subsubtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT-QUERY RESPECTING GOVERNMENT POLICIES
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, certainly I want to associate myself and my party with the condolences expressed by the hon. member to the Right Hon. Leader of the Opposition and to say that that sad event is felt by all of us.
In so far as the reference to the minister in Paris is concerned, 1 am in the process of looking at his speech notes. As I understand it, he was in that forum at the IMF urging measures which would lead to a worldwide recovery and would permit the Canadian economy to recover along with the economies of other major countries. He was pointing out the seriousness of unemployment rates in our country and in all other countries represented in the IMF, and urging particularly that high interest rates prevailing in the United States be addressed so that we all have greater incentive facilities.

subtopic: REQUEST FOR REMOVAL OF TAX ON BUILDING MATERIALS
REQUEST FOR REMOVAL OF TAX ON BUILDING MATERIALS
speechtext: Madam Speaker, my supplementary question is directed to the minister responsible for housing. I am sure that he will know that the unemployment level in the construction industry now stands at 20 per cent, that is, in the order of 150,000 construction workers out of work. It is the worst situation in which the construction industry has found itself in two decades. Also the minister will know that the Canadian construction industry has repeatedly asked the federal government either to withdraw or seriously reduce the federal tax on construction materials. The construction industry regards that as fundamental to stimulating its economy and the economy as a whole. Does the minister support its request and, if so, what will he do with it? If not, why not?

speakeroldname: Hon. Paul J. Cosgrove (Minister of Public Works):
speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
subtopic: REQUEST FOR REMOVAL OF TAX ON BUILDING MATERIALS

Madam Speaker, in anticipation of the challenge to the industry and the strength of the demand for units in the country this year, particularly multiple units, the government decided, rather than adopt the step just mentioned by the hon. member for Rosedale, to include funds in the budget of last November which would be of direct and massive assistance to getting multiple construction of units. This is why, for example, $350

May 11, 1982

million was designated to start the construction of 15,000 units of rental accommodations across Canada and why, for example, just a few weeks ago, that 15,000 units were accelerated with a commitment to start the construction of 30,000 rental units in the country this year, depending upon the ability and the response of the industry to take up those funds. We think that that $350 million, compared with the small benefit of the other tax incentive which is being talked about, is much more significant and much more useful.

subsubtopic: INCREASE IN NUMBER OF SMALL BUSINESS FAILURES- REQUEST FOR SHORT-TERM FUNDING
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, my third supplementary is to the Minister of State for Small Business and Tourism. I am sure the minister is aware that small and medium-sized businesses have suffered very badly during the current recession. Indeed, the figure now stands at 3,651 bankruptcies in the first four months of this year alone.
The small business organizations have repeatedly asked the minister if he would establish emergency short-term loans under the Small Businesses Loans Act. Does the minister intend to act on their request, or will he continue to refuse to do so?

speakeroldname: Hon. Charles Lapointe (Minister of State (Small Businesses and Tourism)):
speakerposition: Minister of State (Small Businesses and Tourism)
subsubtopic: INCREASE IN NUMBER OF SMALL BUSINESS FAILURES- REQUEST FOR SHORT-TERM FUNDING
speechtext: Madam Speaker, I agree with the hon. member that small businesses are suffering as a result of the present state of the economy. However, the hon. member will recall that as far as the Small Businesses Loans Act is concerned, in 1981, 19,600 small Canadian businesses received guaranteed loans from the federal government under this legislation, an increase of 31 per cent over the previous year. I think we are making a serious effort to promote the use of programs available to small businesses, and according to the response from this sector, it is clear that utilization of these programs has increased.

subsubtopic: QUALITY OF RAILS PRODUCED BY SYDNEY STEEL CORPORATION
speechtext: Madam Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Transport. He knows that unemployment is rampant in Cape Breton and that thousands of workers in that area of the province of Nova Scotia are dependant upon Sydney Steel Corporation and its success. Therefore I would ask the minister about his statements, which have been widely reported, questioning the quality of the rails being produced at Sydney Steel Corporation, which are rigidly inspected. The company has enjoyed a national and international reputation for quality rails. What evidence does the minister have to back up or justify his counterproductive statements? Can he produce any tangible evidence of current bad quality and, more important, can he say when any of these alleged deficiencies were brought to the attention of SYSCO management, and has he bothered to check? As well, what about the deleterious effect on the company, its work force, and its future prospects?

subsubtopic: QUALITY OF RAILS PRODUCED BY SYDNEY STEEL CORPORATION
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, this is something which is well known by the people at SYSCO. The proof of it is simply the fact that CN has been forced, because of these circumstances, to reduce the level of rail purchases from the SYSCO plant.
The management of SYSCO has asked for another meeting with the CN management on that subject. This will take place. CN accepts the current proposal that an independent assessor be appointed in order to determine the degree of technical difficulty encountered by SYSCO in the production of some types of rail.

subsubtopic: QUALITY OF RAILS PRODUCED BY SYDNEY STEEL CORPORATION
speechtext: Madam Speaker, I want to take issue in a most respectful and vigorous way with what the minister has said. I would question the basis of his information.

Madam Speaker,
I would ask the minister again about the rails which are imported by Canadian National from other countries. Can the minister explain why Sydney Steel Corporation was never given an opportunity to tender on these rails or be informed of any specifications which made them unique, if in fact they are so, so that it also would have an opportunity to manufacture them and further the company's future?
Would he not agree that it would be more appropriate for him to concentrate on arranging more CN rail orders instead of making these counter-productive statements which can only keep the work force in Cape Breton from achieving not only orders for the CN, but for other customers as well? The reputation of SYSCO has been badly damaged by the minister, and I think he should verify his facts, because any problems which existed with Sydney Steel rails were in 1980 and
May 11, 1982

most of the rails involved were re-inspected and accepted by CN. In any event, the rails are now the best that have ever been produced there, and they are nothing to be ashamed of in any way, shape or form.
Hear, hear!
Madam Speaker, if my hon. friend insists on talking and thinking the way he does, it is okay with me. He can go on. Unfortunately, however, the facts are different.
You do not know the facts.

In 1980-81, CN was purchasing 151,000 tons of rail from SYSCO. In 1982 it was brought down to 97,000 tons, while 11 per cent of CN's needs in 1981-82 were purchased abroad. This, again, is something it does when it has to, when the two Canadian plants, SYSCO and Algoma, cannot provide CN with the quantity or quality it needs. CN has to operate a railway. It has to be certain that the track it buys will stand the wear and tear of everyday operation. It has to do that in the interest of safety. Please bear this in mind. In 198283, CN will purchase 88,000 tons of rail, none from outside the country. Again, CN only purchases rail outside Canada when it cannot avoid it. That is all.

speechtext: Madam Speaker, my question is directed to the Prime Minister. Yesterday in Paris, the Minister of Finance suddenly discovered-abroad-that unemployment was a problem here at home. If the Minister of Finance is at long last saying that unemployment is the number one priority here in Canada or ought to be, with more than a million Canadians unemployed and a record level of unemployment since the great Depression, does the Prime Minister have a single new job-creating program to announce to the people of Canada?

A couple of days earlier we had announced increased funding for construction of rental housing and renovation of existing houses, totalling $130 million, a matter which was just referred to in an earlier answer given by the minister responsible for housing. If independent action is not taken, this will have devastating implications for many economies around the world, as the Prime Minister knows.
Considering that Francois Mitterrand brought in special programs for home owners, for small businessmen, and also for other sectors of the French economy, and considering that Chancellor Schmidt of the Germany added between $3 billion and $4 billion to provide additional stimulus some two months ago to the German economy, does the Prime Minister now have anything new, of this magnitude, to offer the people of Canada, or will he just reannounce the same old stuff?

speechtext: I appeal to the hon. member. Why is he claiming as a recent announcement measures taken several months ago by these two heads of governments, whereas ours were announced in the past few weeks and, incrementally, they are as significant as anything done over there.

speechtext: Madam Speaker, the matter is very simple. It is twofold. First, the action they took was some time ago, which means they recognized unemployment as a serious issue well ahead of this government. Second, the impact of their programs in terms of their economies is all out of proportion to what this government has announced. They are not trying to nickel-and-dime their countries to death and pretend they are doing something; they are doing something.

My final question to the Prime Minister is as follows. There are three constituencies in Canada, namely, Timiskaming, Broadview-Greenwood, and Leeds-Grenville which are not represented in the House of Commons, one since as long ago as Christmas when it lost its member, and two since then. speechtext:
Madam Speaker, my question is for the Secretary of State for External Affairs. He will know that Pretoria and Washington seem to be combining to hold up as long as they possibly can, if not forever, the independence of Namibia, which the minister himself said last November he hoped to see come about this year in accordance with the UN resolution. Can the minister explain why Canada, as a member of the contact group, is not
Oral Questions
protesting in the most strenuous way possible the manner in which various electoral systems are being proposed? First of all there is the suggestion that there be one person with two votes, and of course SWAPO turned that down; and they are now proposing there be one person with one vote but each vote be counted twice. As the minister knows, all these devices are contrary to what we should be pressing for in the contact group. I ask the minister are we pressing for or is there any hope of having a genuinely democratic system in Namibia of one person, one vote?

speakeroldname: Hon. Mark MacGuigan (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: NAMIBIA-SELECTION OF ELECTORAL SYSTEM
speechtext: Madam Speaker, as the hon. member knows, there are a great many valid electoral systems in the democratic world. In each case it is important that the system be devised with the needs of the people in mind. Namibia is a country in which there are a great many different groups, none of which, I understand, comprises as much as half the population. Therefore it is important to get an electoral system which gives some weight to all of the various groups in that country. That is what the contact group has been trying to facilitate with its various proposals. It is not open to me to discuss those proposals in this formula, but we have been trying to facilitate the process. This is not a process which involves bad faith on anyone's part, as some have alleged, or some kind of blindness to the needs of the situation. Indeed, it is an attempt to meet the needs of the situation exactly.

speechtext:
1.	Has the government made reference to an economic strategy based on megaprojects and, if so (a) which projects (b) what are the projections for the next 20 years (c) where will they be located (d) under which sector of the economy will they come (e) what is their (i) total (ii) individual value (f) for (i) all projects (ii) each project, what industrial benefits are forecasted for Canada's economy (g) for (i) all projects (ii) each project, how many jobs will be created?

subsubtopic: ECONOMIC STRATEGY
speechtext:
1. (a)
The government has not made reference to an economic strategy based exclusively on megaprojects. The government in its policy paper entitled "Economic Development for Canada in the 1980's", tabled at the time of the November budget, stated that the 1980s hold great promise, offering opportunities of unprecedented magnitude and the potential for lasting benefits from economic renewal. Specifically, the policy paper set out three areas of major opportunity:
(i)	the development of our natural resources; energy, food products, such as grain and fish, forest products and minerals, such as coal and potash.
(ii)	the second area of economic development opportunity lies in manufacturing activity. The paper cites the published report of the Major Projects Task Force which identifies $440 billion in potential projects predominantly in the energy and resource sectors, noting the opportunity presented to the manufacturing sector to both supply machinery, equipment and materials needed for resource development and to extend the further processing of resource products beyond the primary stage.
(iii)	the third area of growth is in the innovation, development and exploitation of advanced technology and high productivity goods and services. The paper notes that Canadian creativity has proven in the manufacturing, engineering and service areas, such as nuclear technology, aerospace, communications, electronic data processing, retailing and urban transportation equipment, that we can place ourselves at the forefront of technological change in selected world markets. It is equally clear, however, that we must build upon and strengthen our technological infrastructure.
(b) The major project task force report of June, 1981, provides an inventory of specific projects tc the year 2000 having a cost of $100 million or more. The government in October, 1981, published a major capital projects inventory containing projects with an investment value of more than $100 million. These projects were divided into categories of "committed", "planned" or "possible" to the year 1990

May 11, 1982
Order Paper Questions
depending upon the status of industry plans. The government inventory also provides an address list of all the sponsor companies, including a contract name and other relevant project information. It is intended, if industry agrees it would be useful, to annually up-date this inventory. Canadian industry is therefore to be kept appraised of possible current and future opportunities arising from major projects.
(c)(d)(e)(f) The two above-mentioned publications not only set out a project, specific inventory of currently identified projects, but as well set out the costs, projected employment where known and sectoral and regional distribution of the project inventory. It is expected that the massive investment in these resource development projects will generate many billions of dollars worth of opportunities for supplying these projects or developing new resource-based products.
2.	In order for Canadian industry and workers to benefit to the maximum extent possible from major activity the federal government announced new initiatives in August, 1981. These initiatives were (i) the announcement of industrial benefits objectives and guidelines for owner-sponsors of major projects,
(ii)	the creation of an office of industrial and regional benefits within the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce; and
(iii)	the formation of a committee on industrial and regional benefits replacing the existing advisory committee on industrial benefits. These measures are intended to increase the federal government's ability to identify and stimulate industrial benefits associated with, in particular, the development of Canada's natural resources. They also respond to a need to have a system in place to administer the industrial benefits provisions of Bill C-48.
With respect to supplier development, a critical role must be played by project sponsors. The government will encourage sponsors to put in place policies and practices that ensure that Canadian suppliers benefit from supplier development activities that are seen as good procurement strategy in many industries. These include phased contracts, performance milestones, early definition of requirements, participation in start-up costs, assistance with technical or managerial skills, etc.
3.	The government, through Crown corporations, may invest in some megaprojects. The level and nature of investment in any specific project will depend upon several factors, including the magnitude of the project and the role which the project plays in the achievement of national economic objectives. For example, through Petro-Canada the government may invest in major energy projects which have the potential to add significantly to Canada's domestic oil supplies, and thus contribute to the achievement of oil self-sufficiency. The precise nature of each Crown corporation's investment will depend upon its nature and financial situation.
It is not possible at this time to estimate how much the government will invest in the several projects listed in the major capital projects inventory. Many of these projects are still in a preliminary planning stage, and even those in an
advanced stage of planning may not yet have received full review by regulatory bodies and government departments to determine whether they are consistent with the public interest.
It also is not possible at this time to predict the precise form which government financial participation might take. Crown corporations will participate as equity investors in some projects. In other cases, the government may provide tax and direct incentives. The form of the government's participation will be dependent upon, inter alia, its judgment as to the national economic benefits to be derived from the project, the capability and willingness of private sponsors to assume the associated risks, the financial benefits to be derived by Crown corporations from investments, and the impact of different forms of participation such as tax expenditures upon related government policies and programs.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-EFFECT OF ECONOMIC POLICIES ON SMALL BUSINESSES
speechtext:
That this House, alarmed by the fact that over 1,500,000 Canadians are unemployed and aware that small businesses generate more than 60 per cent of all new jobs created in Canada, condemns this government for its ruinous economic policies, particularly those contained in the budget, which have effectively destroyed the spirit of entrepreneurship in the small business community, have contributed substantially to the loss of job-creating opportunities and which have drastically diminished investment in Canada.
He said: Mr. Speaker, in commencing debate on this important motion, let me waste no time in stating that it is difficult to exaggerate the sense of rage, frustration and anger felt in the Canadian small business community as a result of the disastrous economic policies which are being pursued by this government. That vital sector of our economy which we call the small business community has special qualities which distinguish it from other economic groups in our society.
The Canadian small businessman and woman have the characteristic of being the risk-takers flowing from their belief in the free enterprise system. This economic group creates 60 per cent of all new jobs in Canada. These men and women believe in the values of initiative, incentive and the spirit of entrepreneurship. These traits which are the hallmark of the small business community of our society are being sapped because of government interference and ill-conceived economic policies.
From the small service company in the petroleum industry in western Canada to the manufacturer of auto parts in Ontario to the small vessel construction industry in Atlantic Canada, the over-all outlook for prosperity is grimmer than it ever has been since the bleak days of the depression.
In normal times, statistics demonstrate that one-half of all small businesses fail in the first two years. Further, four out of five businesses are unsuccessful after five years. This is primarily because of under-capitalization of the enterprise, mismanagement or a combination of both. But in today's economic climate, superimposed on these factors the small businessman and woman must contend with punishing interest
May 11, 1982
rates and a budget that snuffs out any sense of incentive. It is not enough for me to speak in terms of bold generalities. I wish to direct my attention to certain aspects of the budget which are presently having a crippling effect on small business people and must be changed.
In a budget which was replete with policies that extinguish incentives and one's personal sense of enterprise, no proposal was more destructive in the budget for the small business person than the decision to tax dividends by a distribution tax of 12.5 per cent.
The small business rate of taxation is normally 25 per cent, subject to provincial variations. But the effect of this proposal will actually raise the corporate tax on active business to thirty three and one-third per cent when funds are paid out of dividends.
Let me illustrate a typical situation by way of specific example prepared for me by a pre-eminent tax lawyer. Let us assume we have a small businessman who has a non-working wife. He has two children both under the age of 18 years. The businessman draws $2,000 a month for living expenses and when profits allow he takes $10,000 in dividends. Let us assume that the gross income from the business is $39,000 including the payment of dividends. In comparing this factual information on the basis of a 1981 return with that of a tax return which must be filed in 1982 pursuant to the provisions of the budget, there is a 10.1 per cent increase in the tax payable by such a small business person. This is so even after including the benefit of indexing and the change in the tax credit.
Thus we have the following incredible situation. We have a gross income in these two years which is exactly the same. But inflation has to be taken into account. Therefore, the purchasing power of that income is reduced in the second year, that is in 1982, by 12 per cent or more. In addition there is an increase in tax of 10.1 per cent. This is a common situation. The numbers I have used are conservative-and I use that word in the best sense-namely $2,000 by way of a draw and $10,000 taken out at the end of the year when profits allow.
A second and equally important example of a policy that works to the detriment of a small-business man pertains to the treatment of capital cost allowance. The new provisions cut the write-off in half in the year of the asset in which it is acquired. The Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen), in a piece of propaganda that was sent out to 200,000 small business people in Canada, stated that the change in depreciation write-off in the first year "merely alters the timing of the depreciation". This is simply not true. Let me give an example to back it up.
For depreciable property there is what is known as class 12 write-offs. Class 12 write-offs apply to restaurateurs, doctors, plumbers, electricians and to people who have small tools. In my community there is restaurant called "The Mill". Assume that restaurant has breakage amounting to $500 a month. Taken over a year, it totals $6,000. Formerly under class 12

May 11, 1982

depreciable property a person was entitled to write off the total amount of breakage, but that amount is now cut in half.
Let us take a look at another illustration. A small businessman or woman wishes to purchase a building for $500,000. The capital cost allowance is 5 per cent. In year one, the owner of that building under pre-budget conditions would write off $25,000. Under the provisions of the budget, a person is entitled to write off only $13,500. At the end of ten years, the difference in deductions is $7,878.12. That is the difference after ten years and yet the Minister of Finance says it is only a matter of timing.
I want to pause for a moment to make a point. I am concerned that there is no one in this House who has not received, quite rightly and quite justifiably, many protests from the insurance industry. The insurance industry has mobilized a blitzkrieg which would make Hitler pale. There is going to be a change in the budget as a result of the pressure that has been applied by people with insurance policies who have been writing to their Members of Parliament. They have also been phoning their Members of Parliament. It is very easy to understand the inequity of the situation which occurs when a person has to pay income tax on a benefit he or she has not received. That is easy for anyone to understand. But my concern with respect to the Minister of Finance is that most people do not understand what capital cost allowance is. It is complicated but it is essential and important to the small business community. Most Canadians do not understand what dividends are, the taxation and the effect of dividends. My concern is that people will not understand.
Only political pressure, I think, will initiate any change in this disastrous budget. But for the small business community which is the backbone of our economy, in spite of the good work by the John Bullochs, and the Jim Bennetts, by our party and the other party to my left, in terms of pressuring the government, I do not see the Minister of Finance moving from his position.
I want to use one more illustration because I want to make the point that although some of these matters are very complicated, they are very, very important. The third illustration of duplicity and inconsistency in government policy applies to the raising of the limits from $750,000 to $1 million in terms of retained earnings for a company to qualify as a small business for the preferred rate of tax. While the raising of the limit is to be welcomed, in my opinion it does not go nearly far enough to take into consideration inflation. Dividends paid out of retained earnings will no longer cause a reduction in retained earnings for the purposes of tax.
Again I wish to give an illustration. Suppose company A and company B were set up in 1975, each earning $100,000 per year and paying $25,000 in taxes. Further suppose that company A annually pays dividends out of its funds, whereas company B retains all its earnings. If company B shareholders pay out the retained cash after budget night, they will be subject to a corporate distribution tax of $50,000. Further, company B has cumulative deductions of $600,000 as of
Supply
January 1, 1982, leaving only $400,000 available for the small business deduction.
The point is that every Liberal minister of finance has encouraged small business people of Canada to retain earnings within the company. Now we have a situation where the small business person who has stripped the treasury by way of paying out dividends has a preferred advantage because he has from $1 to $1 million to go, whereas the company that retained earnings in the circumstances is in a less preferred position. In addition, the company that has abided by government policy in terms of retained earnings, if he wants to take it out by way of dividends, will have to pay the 12.5 per cent tax on dividends. I think this is totally wrong. Despite the fact that it is complicated, I insist that the Minister of Finance pay attention to it because it is one factor which has provided disincentive to the small business community.
During the course of the budget debate a document was sent out to 200,000 small business people in Canada. It was replete with fraudulent statements and inaccuracies; it was a piece of propaganda. I have given three illustrations of where it is incorrect, one being the 12.5 per cent tax dividend and the other the statement that investors will pay less tax. That is just absolute nonsense, and patently so. It is absolutely not the case that changes in depreciation or write-offs do not have a significant effect upon small businesses.
One of the hallmarks of the system of taxation has always been the confidentiality of the tax returns of taxpayers, yet the 200,000 recipients of this piece of propaganda received this brochure as a result of the computers of Revenue Canada being utilized for the purpose. If that is not a formal breach of the Income Tax Act, it is a tremendous violation of the spirit of the act. Whether or not a person is a prostitute or whatever, everyone is compelled to disclose their income. The quid pro quo is that no one will know about it except if a person lies or commits a fraud, yet the Minister of Finance utilized the facilities of Revenue Canada for this purpose. It does not surprise me; it is consistent with the conduct of the government. I register my protest with respect to the way this political propaganda was disseminated.
I have tried to illustrate, by the examples I have given, the betrayal in specific terms of risk-takers and small entrepreneurs, those people with incentive who have traditionally been the backbone of our economy. Although the ways and means necessary to implement the policy outlined in the budget have not been passed, there is no sign that the Minister of Finance is willing to change his posture.
As of Friday, Statistics Canada told us that there were officially 1.2 million Canadians unemployed, yet we know that the real figure is closer to 1.5 million. My community is in the heartland of southwestern Ontario. In Cambridge we have 17.5 per cent registered unemployment. We have gone from a situation where there has never been any question of employment in Cambridge to a situation where one out of five men and women cannot obtain jobs. We have 14,000 people from Portugal and 15,000 people from Newfoundland who came to

May 11, 1982
Supply
Cambridge because they could always find employment; it is in the industrial heartland of Ontario. We also know that with respect to new jobs 60 per cent are created by the small business community.
In an excellent speech which was given by Mr. J. K. Gray, vice-president of Canadian Hunter Exploration Limited, he referred to the United States senate committee which in its recent investigation concluded that 97 per cent of new jobs being created in the United States were created by companies that did not make it into the list of the top 1,000 in Fortune . magazine. A report of the Massachusetts Institute of Technology demonstrated that small firms with 20 or fewer employees generate 66 per cent of all new jobs in the United States. This dovetails almost precisely with our statistics on small businesses. We need new small companies to create jobs, yet the government established an economic climate which stifles initiative and enterprise.
When massive numbers of people are out of work as they are today, one only has to pick up the morning paper and look at the rocketing number of insolvencies of businesses in Canada. The statistics published by Statistics Canada for the first four months of 1982 show that bankruptcies increased by 37 per cent over the same period last year. In Ontario the number of business bankruptcies increased from 198 to 288 over the first four months. Yet bankruptcies are only one form of insolvency. Previously I told the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Ouellet) that since the change to the Bank Act in the mid-1960s the number of bankruptcies does not fairly represent the number of businesses which have gone broke. This is because of what is known as the floating charge debenture which is utilized by banks today. When a creditor signs a floating charge debenture securing the money borrowed for his small business, it is only between him and the banks, not between the government, the bank and the borrower. What has happened as a result is that the number of insolvencies in Canada today cannot be calculated because we have absolutely no figures. It is my estimation that there are four insolvencies caused by receivership for one bankruptcy.
The reason is that the people who go bankrupt are the people who want to have their debts extinguished after a certain period of time. What normally happens to a businessman when the banker sees that he cannot meet his liabilities as they come due is that the bank walks in and exercises its security. Although people might be reading the morning papers and saying it is tragic that 37 per cent more businesses have gone into bankruptcy, it does not tell the whole story. Receiverships do not include the group of people who have lost faith, who have some money but are not making money and decide to close the doors because there is no economic environment in which they can sell their goods.
There are three categories in this area; those who close the door, those who go into receivership and those in bankruptcy.
There are no statistics available for those people in the first two categories to show how serious the situation really is.
What is a better indicator are the unemployment figures. The reason most people are unemployed is that businesses have either laid them off or shut down. Therefore, unemployment statistics are a better gauge. When you see 17.5 per cent of the people of Cambridge registered with Manpower as unemployed, it gives an indication of how many businesses are shutting down and laying people off.
I will now move on to another point. Our way of life has been guided by this government which has an insatiable appetite for revenue. There is no better illustration of its insatiability than the new provisions of the budget dealing with the use of company cars. I would like to talk about the average Canadian who has the use of a company car for the purposes of his business. The provision with respect to company cars affects thousands of people in every province.
Since it is a complicated measure people do not want to pay attention and examine its details, but it is my duty to explain as simply as possible the ramifications of this proposal. The stand-by charge, which is a technical word for the minimum charge for the personal use of a car, is being raised by 150 per cent if the car is owned by the company; that is, from 1 per cent to 2Vi per cent per month. In the case of leased vehicles, the minimum charge is being increased from two-sixths to five-sixths of the leasing costs of the undepreciated value of an automobile.
Let me expand on that point. Whether the car is being used for five years or ten years, the charge is based on the undepreciated value of that car. There is no consideration of when it is bought or how long it has been used but only of the sticker price of the car at the time of purchase.
Once again, the percentages used in the case of a company owned or leased car will be taken on the basis of the undepreciated value of the automobile, notwithstanding that such a car might be three, four or ten years old.
Let me cite a further illustration of the effect on a $15,000 company car at 1981 and 1982 rates using the stand-by charge. In this case, the amount to be added to income in 1981 would be $1,800. The stand-by charge in 1982 will be $4,500 which must be added to income. For a taxpayer earning $22,000 this will mean a $689 increase in his tax. For a taxpayer earning $35,000 this will amount to a $841 increase. For the income earner in the $60,000 bracket, the increase in tax due to the stand-by charge will be $945.
Under the new provisions of this budget, the taxpayer will have to satisfy the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Romp-key) that the personal revenue he received was less than that minimum charge. To do this, every time an employee uses his company car to go to church or to the grocery store, he had better itemize the mileage. I predict that there will be more cheats and frauds created by reason of this new iniquitous measure respecting the use of company automobiles than on any other aspect of the budget.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-EFFECT OF ECONOMIC POLICIES ON SMALL BUSINESSES

Canadians do not cheat.
May 11, 1982

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-EFFECT OF ECONOMIC POLICIES ON SMALL BUSINESSES
speechtext:
Not with respect to this provision. I ask the hon. member if he would record-because the taxpayer will have to prove it to the Minister of National Revenue-every time he used his car for personal use. Can you imagine Mr. Speaker, the book work necessary and the cost?
Every member of the House knows that punishing interest rates are the most serious problem that small-business men and women have had to contend with. Due to annual inflation of more than 12 per cent, the prospect of interest rates coming down significantly are not good. Just as the Solicitor General (Mr. Kaplan) told the truth about the budget when he called it a disaster, it was refreshing for me to hear the Minister of State for Small Businesses and Tourism (Mr. Lapointe) quoted as saying, "We are fearful that if there were a recovery in the U.S., we are not sure whether we would be able to join the bandwagon."
The minister is correct. Everyone took cognizance last week of the new American statistics, showing that for the first time in 17 years the United States experienced a month where the cost of living actually went down instead of up. There was deflation instead of inflation. Inflation for the first quarter of this year in the United States is running at 3 per cent, and if this trend continues, as economic indications show it will, interest rates will plummet in the United States later this summer. Yet this is not the case in Canada; our prospects are that high interest rates and high rates of inflation will continue unabated while more businesses go broke.
The Small Business Development Bond was established in the Crosbie budget of 1979. The emphasis of that bond was on development and expansion. Its purpose was to give the small business community a cushion against high interest rates and to permit expansion and development. It would accomplish that by giving small business the incentive through cash flow- a term for which the government has no understanding-to purchase machines and increase development. When a business has expansion and development, jobs are then created. But what has this government done? It has made the Small Business Development Bond nothing more than a bail-out bond. The bond is only used in cases of desperation and where it is to the advantage of the bank to bail out a customer who is about to go under. This is just one more illustration of the element of disincentive which exists in this budget.
In order to dramatize the insensitivity of this government, I ask the House to hark back to the comments of the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs, who said; "I cannot accept that businessmen have to rely on the post office to make a living; if they do, they had better find other ways". Could any statement by a minister be more illuminating? If this is an indication of the thinking of this minister, who is in charge of the post office, in his attitude towards small business, surely this demonstrates how impoverished and out of touch the cabinet is with the real world on the street where the small business person is.
I take you back to last summer, Mr. Speaker, when businesses were folding as a result of lack of mail service during
Supply
the postal strike. Almost immediately after the strike ended, the post office was transformed into a Crown corporation and postal rates were raised to 30 cents. The minister is still in charge and responsible for the Crown corporation. In effect, the public-including the small business community-were barely recovering from this serious jolt to the solar prexus when they received a judo chop to the neck in the form of a dramatic postal increase. Even with these increases, there are very few of my constituents who would argue that the postal service has improved.
During the course of my speech I have attempted to enumerate and expand upon in some cases the causes of resentment within the small business community and the public at large.
Mr. Speaker, since I am the first speaker I assume I have longer than 20 minutes?

speechtext: Let me say a word about the Federal Business Development Bank. On February 18 last, the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce and Minister of Regional Economic Expansion (Mr. Gray) came to Cambridge armed with briefing notes about my community. There are 75,000 people who reside in the city of Cambridge alone. It came to light that during the last nine months of last year, the Federal Business Development Bank advanced one loan in the amount of $30,000 within my community. I am not sure of the experiences of other members, but when constituents attended at my offices having been turned down by the chartered banks, the first solution I thought of since reading the government propaganda was to send them to the Federal Business Development Bank. The government has indicated that the bank of last resort was the Federal Business Development Bank. What did we find? Last summer, people in my community of 75,000 were paying interest rates of 25 per cent as opposed to the prime rate, and sometimes more. We found that the Federal Business Development Bank, which charges two points above prime, made one loan.

When the most serious problem facing small businesses today is the drying up of working capital, and the consequent inability of the businessman or businesswoman to meet his or her debts and obligations as they come due, this financing review is desperately needed. How long does the minister-

speechtext:
How long does the minister expect Canadians patiently to listen to this government's empty promises? We on this side of the House pray that this review, whenever it is released, will contain some new measure of help to alleviate the crisis which has developed in the small business community with respect to short-term cash flow problems. That is the problem to which the hon. member for Rosedale (Mr. Crom-bie) alluded during question period today.
The difficulty is that with respect to small businesses, people are not paying small businesses for 90 to 120 days and, in some cases, longer than that. These small businesses go to the banks, they cannot cover the inventory, and they are closing up. This is a serious and desperate problem. In order for small businesses to survive, they must be able to extend credit to their customers. Today, many of our small businesses have reached the extent of their credit lines through chartered banks and there is just no money available for them to finance their operations while waiting for customers to settle their accounts. If they cannot obtain some working capital financing, they must halt their operations, lay off some or all of their work force and wait to collect their accounts receivable.
I am about to conclude my remarks. I wanted to mention a few more things, but I wish to make one last point. I was very impressed by what the hon. member for Kingston and the Islands (Miss MacDonald), the former minister of external affairs, told me in casual conversation after she had stepped down from that portfolio. She said that in her experience while we were in government, the most brilliant man that she had come across was the former external affairs minister in Great Britain, Lord Peter Carrington. He was a leader among leaders in the international community. He was a brilliant man, yet because he had improperly assessed the Argentine invasion of the Falklands, he felt he should resign as a matter of honour. I look to the Solicitor General. When he called the budget a political disaster, he was doing nothing less than telling the truth. In my opinion, he would have served as a far better member, in terms of his own credibility, if he had resigned.
I now look to the minister who is responsible for small business and consider the disastrous shape of the small business community. I like the minister. He is a man of goodwill and a fine man. But I say to him that he has been undercut, dramatically and seriously, by the Minister of Finance and the policies he has implemented. I say to the minister that if he is to retain the credibility and respect I have for him, he had better give serious consideration to tendering his resignation.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-EFFECT OF ECONOMIC POLICIES ON SMALL BUSINESSES
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-EFFECT OF ECONOMIC POLICIES ON SMALL BUSINESSES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we debate a motion today which we in the NDP are happy to
support. We must look at what is going on in this country and realize that we are facing the kind of recession which this country has not seen since the 1930s, just before World War II. Unemployment last month affected 1,233,000 people, or 9.6 per cent of the work force according to Statistics Canada. Added to that are another 250,000 workers who have not been counted because they have given up looking for work as there simply is not any work to be found.
The figures are so large that we cannot really realize what this means. Each one of these people, when he or she worked, was producing goods, was purchasing homes, appliances or clothes, was taking holidays, paying taxes, spending money which would help employ other people. For each of them, unemployment is a disaster. Inflation is running 11.6 per cent; that is higher than it was in 1975 when the government imposed its wage and price controls. Interest on housing mortgages is running at 20 per cent, so it is effectively stopping most Canadians who need homes from being able to purchase them because they cannot afford to carry mortgages at the rates now being charged. The rates now being charged may go up six months or a year from now. The days when people could buy a house knowing that the interest rates they were charged on their mortgages would remain the same for at least five years are long gone. The bank interest rate for the best customer is 17 per cent and, for the ordinary small businessman, it is probably 20 per cent or more.
In April, housing starts were so low that it was projected we would build only 142,000 homes in the year. That figure is down by a third over what we were building until recently. Bankruptcies are up by 45 per cent over the same period last year. In April, 850 companies went bankrupt. The liabilities for outstanding debts from business bankruptcies across Canada rose by 82 per cent from April of last year, to $139 million this year. Let us keep in mind that for every company which went bankrupt, probably five to ten went into receivership or voluntarily closed up because they realized they would not be able to continue to operate successfully.
John Maynard Keynes once said that if a company had to borrow a hundred pounds from a bank, it would really have to worry if it could not pay the money back; but if it could borrow a million pounds from the bank, it became the bank's worry, because the bank could not afford to let the company fail. Those words spoken in jest are very true. We know that a company like Massey-Ferguson owes the banks of Canada hundreds of millions of dollars. The banks cannot afford to let Massey-Ferguson go bankrupt. We know that Dome Petroleum borrowed $1.25 billion last year to buy Hudson's Bay Oil and Gas. We know that if these companies cannot meet their interest payments or pay off their loans on time, the banks will extend their loans because the banks cannot afford to accept that kind of loss.
For the small businessman and for the farmer, there is no such option because the banks are refusing to increase the amount of money they will lend them, as indicated by the
May 11, 1982

bankruptcy figures. Banks are increasing the interest rates which these people have to pay. In fact, the banks are very effectively doubling the collateral they request if the loans are to be continued.
All the indicators show that the Canadian economy is not only in a recession but that it is also being driven into a greater recession, and that that recession will be prolonged.
The minister will tell us, as the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) has frequently told us, that all industrial countries are faced with severe economic problems. It appears that Canada's economy is in a more pronounced recession than any of the other industrialized countries and that any improvement in business conditions will be delayed and lag behind the other economies.
The Chase Econometrics Association has predicted for 1982 a real growth in gross national product of 2.6 per cent in France, 2.3 per cent in West Germany, 2 per cent in Japan and 1.5 per cent in Britain. What does it predict for Canada? A decline of seven-tenths of 1 per cent.
This tends to show that our high interest rate policies, advocated and carried out on the advice of the Governor of the Bank of Canada and successive finance ministers, Liberal as well as Conservative in the short period when the Conservatives were in power, are not helping the economy to move out of the recession. Moreover, they do not seem to contribute toward solving the problem of inflation which, according to the most optimistic estimates, can only fall to about 10 per cent for the next year.
High interest rates coupled with a high rate of inflation hits small business people especially hard. The record number of bankruptcies reached in March, over 1,000, will likely increase if the necessary policy measures to reduce interest rates are not taken immediately. According to the Canadian Federation of Independent Business, high interest rates are the major factor leading to the decreased profitability and increased number of bankruptcies of small-business men in this country.
In a letter which the president of the Canadian Federation of Agriculture, Glen Flaten, wrote to the Minister of Finance and which was recently circulated to all Members of Parliament, he pointed out that the depressed returns to most of the farming industry mean that the industry cannot support any significant level of indebtedness, even for current operating purposes, at present interest rates. He pointed out previously acquired indebtedness has increased in cost 75 to 100 per cent for many farmers and there is no way it can be repaid at today's prices or at any prices which farmers are likely to see in the near future.
Farmers and small manufacturing firms that regarded the small business bond policy of tax concessional lending by the banks as a source of hope now find that it was a hoax and a delusion. The policy does not affect any guarantee that the loans would actually be available and imposes overly strict eligibility criteria, which leads to a situation where loans are available only after it is too late for most business people. Moreover, in spite of the high demand for the program,
Supply
Department of Finance officials say that they have not stepped up their spending estimates, set at $20 million compared with $150 million last year.
The Canadian Federation of Agriculture is urgently calling on the government to replace the small business bond with a policy of real substance to face the critical situation which farmers and small businessmen have to cope with. It suggests that the Farm Credit Corporation should be empowered to borrow the quantities needed immediately on a tax concessional basis so that it can lend at 10 per cent interest to the farmers, especially those in difficulty.
The availability of loans to small businesses is an important issue which must and should be dealt with through an efficient mechanism of credit rationing which cannot be left entirely to the willingness of the lender. At present the chartered banks control the allocation of investment funds. We know of the tremendous loans which the chartered banks made to the oil, gas and mining companies in the last year or year and a half. As I indicated earlier, one and a quarter billion dollars was loaned to Dome Petroleum, Inco, Brascan and others. They could get hundreds of millions of dollars to permit them to go ahead with take-overs. At the same time, in the third quarter of 1981, the mining and petroleum industries received 44 per cent of all loans made by chartered banks in the industrial sector. In the same period, business loans to industries under the Small Businesses Loans Act was around 1 per cent of all business loans made by the chartered banks.
As has already been indicated, small businesses employ 60 per cent or more of all workers in this country. The large corporations such as the mining and petroleum industry are capital-intensive and employ a relatively small number of workers. Yet because government policies have encouraged them to do so, the banks made the vast bulk of their loans to the large companies instead of the small entrepreneurs operating in the service sector, manufacturing and agriculture.
The recent changes in the tax system are imposing a heavy burden on small enterprises. As the Financial Times put it in a recent issue, the November 12 federal budget discourages expansion in the small business sector, minimizes the opportunity for equity financing from outside sources, and reduces the market value of each small business.
The problem areas of the budget pointed out by the Canadian Federation of Independent Business are as follows. Interest expense allowable as a tax deduction will be restricted to the amount of income earned from investments during the year. Any excess interest costs will be deferred or will be treated as capital losses, only one-half deductible against capital gains.
Instalment sales require the payment of taxes on the sale immediately rather than when the buyer makes payments. Prior to November 12, 1981 reserves were allowed to all taxpayers in respect of instalment sales where a portion of the proceeds would not be paid until a future date. Only one-half of the normal capital cost allowance is now available to be deducted in the first year. A special tax of 12.5 per cent is imposed on dividends paid by small corporations.

May 11, 1982
Supply
The tax system has become progressively more complex for small businesses already struggling under the avalanche of government red tape. This implies increased professional fees, which small business can ill afford. In this period of crisis, government should intervene to help small business and put a stop to ever-increasing unemployment and the growing number of bankruptcies.
I wish to make a few suggestions to the minister. We suggest the reversal of the high interest policy which is severely hurting small enterprises. We want a comprehensive reform of the tax system as well as a system of industrial incentives to ensure equitable treatment of large and small businesses alike.
We want policies to facilitate the access of small businesses to financial, managerial and technical advice. It is inappropriate to blame small businesses for mismanaging their affairs, as is sometimes done without taking into account the difficulties of access to expertise so readily available to large corporations. In this respect, strengthening of the CASE program is indispensable.
Foreign trade policy should be elaborated to encourage small businesses to sell overseas, thereby promoting exports. A large number of industrial countries, including West Germany and Japan, have programs to help industrial enterprises find markets for their products in foreign countries.
The emphasis of the Export Development Corporation, which has already favoured big business, should be changed to give equal attention to small and medium-sized businesses. Government investment should be redirected and restructured to help the problem areas in a way to create the maximum possible number of jobs.
In government procurement, since governments, federal, provincial and municipal, are between them the biggest purchasers of goods and services, they should be developed so that small enterprises can share in the business and purchases of government.
I should like to say a few words about that infamous pamphlet sent out by the Department of Finance to small-business men, telling them about all the goodies which were in the most recent budget. I am sure the Minister of State for Small Businesses and Tourism (Mr. Lapointe), who is going to follow me, knows that the mailing out of that brochure by the Department of Finance was greeted with unanimous hostility by all the organizations which represent small-business men. They argued, and I think their arguments were sound, that the claims made in that brochure were mostly spurious and false. That brochure was printed at government expense and was sent out from lists procured from Revenue Canada. Mr. Speaker, it may not have been illegal, it may not have been a breach of the confidentiality sections of the Income Tax Act, but if it was not illegal it came as close to being illegal as was possible and it certainly was a violation of the spirit of the act.
I want to tell the Minister of State for Small Businesses and Tourism that when I heard the complaints about that pamphlet and listened to the complaints of the representatives of the Canadian Federation of Independent Business, I thought it
would be a good idea, and only fair, to send out their complaints to the same group of people who got that brochure from the government using the confidential lists of Revenue Canada. Therefore, I wrote to the minister in charge of Revenue Canada. I did not ask him to give me the list; I knew that it would be improper and illegal for him to give me the names and addresses. All I asked him to do was provide me with the same service which he had provided to the Minister of Finance.
I had a mistaken idea, Mr. Speaker-I have been here long enough and I should have known better-that all Members of Parliament are somehow equal. We have all been elected by our constituents and we should all have the same rights and privileges. So I had the idea-which, of course, proved incorrect,-that I could get from Revenue Canada the same kind of service which they provided to the Minister of Finance. But, Mr. Speaker, after a good long time, after five or six weeks, I got back a letter from the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Rompkey) telling me that he could not do for me what he had done for the Minister of Finance.
I was not so concerned that the 200,000 businessmen should know what I thought about the budget; I thought they should know what their own organizations thought about it. But, Mr. Speaker, as I might have expected, as I have learned to expect from Liberal governments, what is good for the government, what is proper for them, is improper for everybody else. So I understand that.
I say to the minister that, as has happened in all democratic countries, there will come a time, not too long from now, when the present Liberal government members will find themselves in the opposition. I will not be surprised if they find that they get the same treatment from whoever is then the government as we receive now. Then they will realize that real democracy means that every person and every elected representative is entitled to the same rights and privileges. When they realize that, we will begin to have a more open, a more honest and a more real democratic form of government than we have at the present time.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome the opportunity to speak in this matter and set the record straight on the efforts of this government to assist the small business community. I listened very carefully to the speeches of my two colleagues, the hon. member for Cambridge (Mr. Speyer) and the hon. member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Orlikow).
If I may deal briefly with what my colleague from Winnipeg North has said, particularly the part of his speech when he told me and the House that he was ready to give me some advice, I would like to give him a few answers to his suggestions. First of all, he spoke of the high interest rate policy. There is no such thing as a high interest rate policy in this country. There is a policy to fight inflation, and one of the means to fight inflation-

Is high interest rates.
May 11, 1982

speakerposition: Minister of State (Small Businesses and Tourism)

speechtext:
-in order to restore a higher level of employment, is to use this mechanism of high interest rates, which is quite similar to the mechanism utilized in the United States and in other countries.
Second, he is seeking that we use more government procurement in order to help small business. I would like to tell him that with regard to this suggestion I fully agree with him. That is why over the last year we have increased by 8 per cent the percentage of Canadian procurement towards small business. Here I quote an article from The Globe and Mail which says that small business increased its share of federal government contracts for purchases of goods and services by 8 per cent to 1.28 billion for the fiscal year ended March 31, 1981. I think this is a sound policy and I am glad that the hon. member for Winnipeg North is supporting it.
He also said that we should review the tax system in order to provide more incentives for investors. I am glad to hear that from the member for Winnipeg North because I can remember quite vividly his leader saying that we should have closed more loopholes, or so-called loopholes, in the last budget.
With regard to fostering the capabilities of the small business community towards exportation, I would like to remind the hon. member that there is such a mechanism in the system to help small businesses export more goods. There is one program particularly which is called the program for development of export marketing, the PDEM program. Approximately 1,000 small businesses have been encouraged under the terms of that program in 1981. So he did not come out with many very exciting new ideas, unfortunately, as is always the case.
With regard to the speech of my colleague for Cambridge, he made the usual plea that the last federal budget of November 12 is going to kill entrepreneurship and kill the small business community. He mentioned two items particularly, the tax on dividends and capital cost allowances. He certainly did forget-as is customary for members opposite-to mention all the special aspects in the Canadian tax system which affect and assist small businesses. One of these aspects-

-Mr. Speaker, is the special income tax rate applied to Canadian small businesses. We all know about this on both the opposition and the government side, but it is conveniently ignored, perhaps because it is a unique advantage in our Canadian economy. When the first $200,000 of a business with a total income of $1 million are taxed at 25 per cent instead of the 46 per cent rate for large corporations, it is not mentioned because, of course, it does not apply in the United States. We conveniently forget that the system is more generous in Canada than in the United States. In the U.S., a small business with an income of up to $75,000 will pay a 30 per cent income tax.
In Canada, as I said before, the first $200,000 of a small business is taxed at 25 per cent. Again, in the United States- people always say that American small businesses are better off than their Canadian counterparts-a small business with
Supply
an income of up to $100,000 is taxed at a rate of 40 per cent. Again, in Canada, the first $200,000 is taxed at 25 per cent. In the United States, all businesses are taxed at a uniform rate of 46 per cent on income over and above $100,000. This is not mentioned because it is a loss of revenue for the government: in other words, the money remains part of the budgets of small businesses, and is either invested or reinvested, representing annually $1.5 billion in revenue that is not collected by the government, because we maintain and shall continue to maintain a special tax system for small businesses.
I looked into the situation in the United Kingdom, France and Australia as far as taxation of small businesses is concerned, and I found that in the U.K., the first $180,000 of a small business's income was taxed at the special rate of 40 per cent, while all other businesses were taxed at a rate of 52 per cent. Of course, all this is not mentioned, because it means that small businesses are getting a very good deal. In his last budget, the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) not only enshrined this practice in the Canadian taxation system but even added a number of improvements. What were these improvements? The minister, before bringing down his budget on November 12, decided to increase the original amount of $175,000, taxed at the special rate of 25 per cent, to $200,000. So that more businesses could qualify for the special income tax rate for small businesses, he raised the maximum cumulative income from $750,000 to $1 million.
There has been no mention, of course, of the fact that under the Canadian tax system, businesses qualifying for the special tax rate for small businesses are entitled to a 25 per cent tax credit-a tax credit, Mr. Speaker, is a refund-on all research and development expenditures. No mention, again, of the fact that under our system, small businesses are entitled to a deferral of up to $200,000 of capital gains resulting from the transfer of small businesses from one generation to the next. Another very popular measure, especially for very small businesses with incomes of up to $50,000 from the manufacture of a product, is exemption from federal sales tax. And still under our system, a little over a year now, unincorporated small businessmen may deduct from their income the salary paid to their spouse. Of course, this does not seem very important to the members opposite, but nevertheless, these incentives to small business represent a loss in revenue of $1 billion a year for the government. Furthermore, in one of the amendments proposed on December 18 to the November 12 budget, at the request of various small business organizations, the Minister of Finance announced that interest costs on investment in small businesses would be deductible, up to $10,000. The amount is exactly the same in the United States. Probably because they forgot to study the budget, the members opposite also forgot to mention that, in the last budget, the Minister of Finance abolished the 5 per cent surtax on small Canadian businesses. They cannot talk about this because it would perhaps show the government in too good a light. They would rather use old horror stories to try and show that small Canadian businesses
