are on the brink of disaster and unable to face today's economic conditions.
I think that Canada's small entrepreneurs are aware of all those incentives. They are also aware of all the programs, subsidies and loan mechanisms of federal government programs in the system and are taking advantage of these opportunities.
As an example, the most recent report of the Conference Board points this out. In the first quarter of 1982 the Conference Board surveyed 4,000 small and medium-sized companies along with its usual panel of 240 large companies. The results appear in its "Survey of Business Attitudes and Investment Spending Intentions" which was published on April 28. Both the government and the private sector recognize how tough international economic conditions are impacting on investment decisions in Canada as in other countries. We do not deny that.
The Conference Board found that the small entrepreneurs in this country are more optimistic than their counterparts in large businesses about their future sales prospects, about increasing employment in their companies by the end of the year and about getting a proper return on their money.
[Translation)
What does this means, Mr. Speaker? It means that businessmen and women, especially in small businesses, are not crybabies like hon. members opposite, but people who have confidence in their country, who are ready to risk their capital and to invest in high technology or service industries to promote a harmonious economic development in Canada.
I agree with my colleagues opposite that the men and the women involved in Canadian small businesses are the backbone of economic development in Canada. There are 1.2 million businesses which qualify as Canadian small businesses. The small business sector accounts for over 40 per cent of all jobs in Canada and for 60 per cent of all new jobs created in 1981. Of course, it is important for the Canadian government to provide these businesses with maximum assistance through its taxation system and its various programs, and I believe that all the examples I gave earlier in my speech show that the taxation system is designed to help small businesses.
I did not even mention yet the various programs developed to help small businesses. I shall begin by the small businesses loans program. During the oral question period today, the hon. member for Rosedale (Mr. Crombie) asked me: Is there a special program which provides advances for small businesses? Under the Small Businesses Loans Act, Mr. Speaker, $502 million was loaned to small Canadian businesses in 1981 with full guarantees from the government. These $502 million was loaned to 17,000 small Canadian businesses under the Small Businesses Loans Act. There is also the small business bond program. The hon. member for Cambridge (Mr. Speyer) indicated that this program was introduced by the Minister of
Finance of the Progressive Conservative government in his budget. That is correct and it was a good program. This is why the Minister of Finance maintained this program in 1981. In 1981 alone, $2.4 billion was loaned to about 13,000 small Canadian businesses under the Small Business Development Bond program.
As you know, Mr. Speaker, under that program banks could grant loans at about half the commercial rate, so in 1981 13,000 small businesses took advantage of the small business development bond, which meant a $2.4 billion investment in the small business sector. What was provided in the recent budget for that program? It was not cancelled, as implied by opposition members. What we have said is that until the November 12 budget, the program was available to incorporated businesses only. We have received numerous requests from the private sector asking us why the program was not made available to all businesses, whether incorporated or not. We also received requests from farmers and fishermen who wanted to be eligible. They wanted the program to be made available to them so they could make ends meet during this difficult period when they have a hard time making their payments because of unduly high interest rates. Well, the Minister of Finance had a positive response, Mr. Speaker, and we introduced the measure called the Small Business Development Bond program that applies to both incorporated and unincorporated businesses, fishermen and farmers alike. We said it would apply to them, because we wanted to help the people in greatest need, businesses, fishermen and farmers in dire straits, instead of promoting business development as was the case in 1981. This is the budget proposal. I would remind you that in 1981, $2.4 billion was loaned at 10 per cent or so to some 13,000 Canadian businesses, and, of course, this is in addition to the 17,000 Canadian businesses that could get loans with a 100 per cent government guarantee, as I said earlier.
In addition to these two programs, Mr. Speaker, there is, of course, the Enterprise Development Program. As you know, it is a program designed to help businesses develop new products, make feasibility studies before marketing new products, improve their performance, and so forth. And in 1981, $329 million was invested in small businesses under the EDP, either as grants of up to 75 per cent of the cost of developing a prototype, either as loan guarantees to help businesses refinance and restructure financially. Some 1,000 businesses benefited from the Enterprise Development Program during the fiscal year 1980-81. And then I can refer to the program for Export Market Development, the so-called PEMD program. And also in 1981, that program enabled some 1,000 Canadian small businesses to seek new markets for their products, either in the United States, Europe or Asia, because the government knows full well that without exports, it would,
May 11, 1982

of course, be very difficult to maintain our production level and increase the number of jobs and small business earnings. I just said that 1,000 businesses benefited from that program during 1981, but after checking my notes, 1 find that the figure is 2,300 Canadian businesses.
I could also mention the Federal Development Bank referred to by the hon. member for Cambridge and the hon. member for Winnipeg North. The Federal Development Bank this year attained a $1 billion total loan volume. Someone may object to my throwing around those huge amounts, because such enormous figures are bewildering but the fact is, Mr. Speaker, that $1 billion is circulating in the Canadian economy as loans from the Federal Business Development Bank. In addition, the Federal Business Development Bank's average loan is known to be $52,000. That gives you an idea of the absolutely phenomenal number of small Canadian businesses which have access to FBDB's loans. Furthermore, small entrepreneurs are aware of the services which are available to them at the Bank, for example the advisory service to small businesses to assist people who are hard pressed or concerned about the future of their business. It is a management assistance program which for a minimal fee will help businesses draw up a development plan expenditure projections and a research strategy for new markets etc. Regarding the seminars and information meetings which are sponsered by the Federal Business Development Bank throughout the country, Mr. Speaker, to help businessmen and women develop their managerial skills, I think they are seldom mentioned, because they are either taken for granted or deemed useless to the community.
I feel that the speeches of my colleagues opposite are too gloomy. Of course, they are expected to play politics and club the government over the head but it seems to me, Mr. Speaker that now and then they should be broadminded enough to see exactly what is going on. I would welcome suggestions but all I hear is: "The budget is no good, withdraw it." In short, that is the gist of what the hon. member for Cambridge has said. Essentially, the hon. member for Winnipeg North said this: We are going to put an end to high interest rates, increase exports and promote investments. Well, Mr. Speaker, everybody, including you, I and all other hon. members are for motherhood. But it would be most refreshing once in a while to hear an hon. member opposite contribute a constructive suggestion to help me, as minister responsible for small business, to define new avenues for the government, which is seeking further solutions to the existing programs. For instance, I hope next fall to introduce amendments to the Small Business Loans Act, but we must first explore several avenues; you just cannot get up one morning and decide on the spur of the moment that you are going to introduce this or that amendment. You must examine the amendment, consider its ramifications, its costs, etc. Should operating costs be included
Supply
and covered by the government's guarantee on chartered bank loans? That is a possibility.
That possibility was not suggested to me be any hon. member opposite. That is the kind of new idea and approach I should like to hear. But because you preside over the proceedings of the House, Mr. Speaker, surely you are bound to hear a great many more speeches than 1 am, and you do realize that unavoidably, whenever there is an allotted day, our hon. friends take up their time trying to find as many faults with the government, hoping that by spreading their loads of halftruths and quoting all sorts of analyses which are out of touch with reality as a whole, they may slowly convince Canadian voters to fall for their tall stories. Unfortunately, today was not yet to be the day when we would be exposed to refreshing and up-dated ideas from hon. members opposite. There is nothing new in their position: Get rid of the budget, they say, and everything will be fine and dandy! I suggest that this is a somewhat simplistic approach to an essentially difficult economic situation.
Mr. Speaker, I have referred to all the tax measures we have introduced to help small businesses. I have mentioned some of the programs provided under the Federal Business Development Bank Act, the Small Business Loans Act, and the Small Business Development Bonds act. I have failed to mention the Department of Regional Economic Expansion which, only last year, subsidized small businesses in Canada to the tune of $280 million. But the fact is, there are so many good programs that there is not enough time to deal with them all. Yet, we know that through briefings and by way of the offices of the Federal Business Development Bank the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce, and the Department of Regional Economic Expansion in all parts of Canada, Canadian men and women involved in business activities have access to these programs.
Further to the administrative reorganization announced by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) on January 11, when the two main economically oriented departments were merged, we want to go one step further, Mr. Speaker, and use all the programs of the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce, all the programs of the Department of Regional Economic Expansion, and their regional offices, and even in due course, in a second stage, use the 103 offices of the Federal Business Development Bank across the country, to bring the services of the government of Canada to the very doorstep of the businessmen and businesswomen, so that they need not come from various parts of the country to the large cities or Ottawa, but that they may find in their own regions what services the Canadian government offers them. That is the orientation, Mr. Speaker, we are giving the administrative restructuring announced last January. And it is with that purpose in mind that we want our programs to have a regional character so that everyone might have equal access to them.

May 11, 1982
Supply
All these programs, new initiatives, and new taxation measures of the Canadian government not only provide strong support for Canadian small businesses, but also reflect a number of basic principles which guide the decisions made by the government to promote continuous development of the private sector. The first of these basic principles is, of course, a free enterprise system which gives Canadian small businesses equal opportunities to compete on the market. The second principle is a firm commitment by the Canadian government to promote the growth and the development of small and medium-size businesses, and I have already mentioned the programs which now aim at meeting this objective. The third principle is to create a dynamic economic environment in which small and medium-size businesses can start, survive and grow. The fourth principle is to make a fair assessment of the problems faced by small and medium-size businesses and to develop effective policies to assist them. This is why we are constantly trying to adjust our programs to existing conditions. Finally, we want to ensure equitable chances for small and medium-size businesses as far as supply opportunities and availability of government information, programs and services are concerned. As I have already explained, we have not only increased to 40 per cent the purchases of the Canadian government, which represents $1.28 billion a year, but we have also attempted to provide equal opportunities for all businesses by making the Canadian government services available to entrepreneurs and businessmen and women. Finally, we want to create a spirit of co-operation between all economic agents to ensure the development of small and medium-size businesses. In this respect of course members opposite try to suggest that there is no consultation between the business community and the government.
Mr. Speaker, sometimes I wish that hon. members opposite would participate in our consultations throughout the country. I was myself in Saint-Georges-de-Beauce last evening and I met with 200 businessmen and women to discuss the economic situation as well as existing government programs and the way to improve them. I must say that what I hear from Canadian men and women in business are not complaints such as those which I hear today but rather messages of optimism, messages which say: Try to support us with your programs, and we, the businessmen and women of Canada, shall do the rest because we believe in this country and in the economy of Canada. I wish hon. members opposite would believe the same things, Mr. Speaker.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to mention a couple of things by way of introduction. The Minister of State for Small Businesses and Tourism (Mr. Lapointe) spent a great deal of time elaborating on the position of the opposition as being opposed for the sake of objecting, for being crybabies, for not being optimistic and for not offering tangible programs for the future, instead of-and I assume this is what
he means-supporting the disastrous programs of the present government.
I remind the House and the minister that on April 27, as reported in the Montreal Gazette, he said:
We're fearful that if there were a recovery in the U.S. we're not sure we would be able to join the bandwagon.
That is the statement of the minister, the optimistic minister who said that even if there is a recovery in the United States we in Canada would not be able to benefit. The minister also noted that while the inflation rate in the United States had dropped to 6.8 per cent, it remains at 11.6 per cent in Canada. The minister goes on in his optimistic way by saying:
Consumer prices in Canada rose at an annual rate of 13.6 per cent in March while they dropped 3.3 per cent in the U.S.
The minister still in his optimistic way went on:
-the recession is severely hurting all levels of the economy from the retail sectors to manufacturing and that consumer and foreign investor confidence is decreasing.
I see the minister is leaving the House at this time. The minister went on to say:
-studies show only about 37 per cent of Quebec businesses are aware of federal government programs-
Here is a government that causes us to be concerned that we might be critical when here in Canada we are experiencing the fact that small businesses account for 23 per cent of provincial sales. There were 8,055 corporate bankruptcies in Canada in 1981. Small business sales were $112 billion-obviously a crucial factor in economic growth-up 21 per cent from 1980 and up 43 per cent from 1979. And the minister says that we are critical, that we are not optimistic.
I remind the Minister of State for Small Businesses and Tourism that the industrial production change is down from 7.8 per cent from one year ago; that urban housing starts are down 17.1 per cent from a year ago; new orders for durable goods are down 10.3 per cent from a year ago; and the unemployment rate is standing at 9.6 per cent, which is a post-war record. The Consumer Price Index-in other words, inflation-is up 11.6 per cent from a year ago; steel output is down 16.2 per cent.
What is there to be optimistic about in Canada? When will this government get through its head that there is a national emergency? Let me put on the record for the government some statements made by the Canadian organization of small business and the Canadian Federation of Independent Business. I will use just a few of them; they came in the wake of the disastrous government budget, and I cite six of them:
1.	Restrict the cash flow for businesses facing excruciating pressures financing capital expenditures at high interest rates.
5. Increase massively professional fees for small businesses that must cope with more than 165 technical tax amendments.
6. Threaten estate planning for small businesses.
2.	Increase the tax burden on investors in small corporations.
3.	Discriminate unfairly against professionals who are unable to incorporate.
4.	Restrict the ability of entrepreneurs to provide for their own retirement.
May 11, 1982

On and on it goes, yet the minister expects us to be optimistic here in Canada. Behind those stark, cold four-digit figures on bankruptcies and business failures you will find not only boarded up store fronts, locked doors of businesses and disconnected telephones, Mr. Speaker, but ruined businesses. You will find men who have had their lives ruined and women who have been driven out of business. You will also find broken personal dreams of thousands of families, mothers, fathers and children whose lives may now be irreparably damaged through no fault of their own.
One of our largest corporations in the city of Peterborough wrote a letter to me and I was asked to bring it to the attention of the government. This letter was written by the president of this corporation and says:
What in fact this new budget does is not to penalize the rich, but rather eliminates the middle-class business or professional who risks, through borrowed funds, money to be invested in speculative or growth ventures that will likely not pay dividends for some years. In fact, the budget proposal on interest deductibility benefits the rich. Wealthy individuals, out of their cash reserves, write a cheque-people like myself must borrow the money to make the same type of investment.
We are not at the stage either through age or inherited wealth to use capital already accumulated for investment purposes.
The net result of this budget, from my point of view, is very clear. I will dispose of all investments in which the interest is non-deductible and will further ignore any equity positions and concentrate on cash savings as the years go on.
Ele concluded by saying:
I am concerned that there is a philosophy behind this budget change that is extremely concerning. By eliminating younger investors who contribute to Canada's growth, the government will be in a much more advantageous position to take over more segments of the private sector, since, in effect, they have removed any entrepreneurial spirit from the younger business and professional class. If that is their intention, then they should have fully stated that in their philosophy behind interest deductibility.
So as not to be accused of only quoting the comments of the president of a major corporation in Canada, I will quote a couple of paragraphs from a letter by Mr. Jack McGee, a Chevrolet-Oldsmobile-Cadillac dealer in Peterborough, which was directed to the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen). He wrote:
Not once in my nearly 34 years of employment have I ever drawn unemployment insurance, not once have I ever failed to pay my income tax on time, not once have I ever bounced a cheque or missed a payment to cover private or government obligations. I am not, nor was not unique; millions of Canadians perform in exactly the same manner!
He went on to write:
It wasn't enough that they got their share every month and every year without any investment. Now they wanted a share of my profit of after tax dollars that I owned and they still wanted to tax me on my retirement money that we were going to use to live on for the rest of our lives.
He continued:
We don't need "empire builders'' in government. Where we need them is in the private sector where jobs should be created. This logically creates more of those income taxes that you need so badly.
He concluded:
I will close with this plea which hopefully you will read and consider before you make your way back to Ottawa.
I ask the Government of Canada to be responsible to its citizens. I ask the Government of Canada to be aware of the importance of the free enterprise
Supply
system to the continuance of Canada's growth. I ask the Government of Canada to be mindful of the system of government we enjoy and expect-a democracy led by representatives elected by their peers to carry out the wishes of the majority of their constituents.
I sent copies of that letter to every Liberal Member of Parliament.
Turning to a small manufacturer in Peterborough, Peterboro Culvert-of course; the budget is disastrous to every sector of our economy-I should like to quote from a letter signed by Mr. J. Wallace Finnie, president of the firm:
We are presently endeavouring to diversify our line and are tooling up to make grain bins for the agricultural market, but with decline in cash reserves it is difficult to finance this type of venture. Government assistance in this area is so uncertain, as to be considered detrimental.
I present this situation to you in order that you, as our representative, may make the government aware of the deterioration that has taken place particularly in the past four or five months, among small business concerns such as ours. I feel that the government has mishandled, misunderstood and is apathetic in its handling of the affairs of the Canadian people.
I received a telephone call today from the vice-president of Silverwood Industries Limited. His office is in Toronto but its head office is in London, Ontario. It was announced today in a press release that because business conditions were not viable and government programs failed to make small business ventures attractive, it was closing its milk producing plant in Peterborough and laying off the staff involved. Silverwood Dairies, a company which does $500 million worth of business per year in Canada, cannot make viable a business in a community the size of Peterborough because the government has failed to make it attractive. As a result there was a net loss of $3.5 million on that amount of volume.
The Minister of State for Small Businesses and Tourism said that we are crybabies and that we are complaining unnecessarily. To use his words, he said: "Small businesses are aware of all the benefits they derive from our fantastic budget." This is a lot of nonsense! People are not prepared today to invest as the minister would have us believe. This is the principal reason $13.5 billion left the country for more favourable climates. For example, in the oil and gas industry, money has flowed south. Why are they investing in Montana and Texas, but not in Alberta which would provide spin-off effects and jobs in Ontario? They are investing in the United States because they receive a return on their investment. They do not fear government expropriation, government take-over and a national policy which puts more and more control in the hands of government and less and less control in the hands of the business community.
We must remember it is cold comfort for thousands of families-wives, husbands and children-that the government is still dithering around six months after its budget in massive, collective confusion over what on earth it can do to retrieve something from a budget which has been roundly and soundly condemned in virtually every sector and quarter of the Canadian economy. The Minister of Finance, who looks more dangerously unnerved each passing day, cries that Canada's hands are tied, that she is prey to the winds of inflation and tight

May 11, 1982
Supply
money blowing over the border and that the flexibility of government is limited by circumstances at large in the western industrialized world. This is nothing but feeble excuse-making and deception.
There is much the Government of Canada could do to eliminate hardships presently experienced by a very large segment of Canadians. The House should ponder very carefully the key elements which rightly preoccupy us today- unemployment at 1.5 million, inflation at 11.6 per cent, interest rates over 17 per cent and real wages declining for the fifth year in a row. To alleviate its dismal performance record, a performance record which is much worse than that of the United States, this government constantly maintains that our fortunes rise and fall. The only departure from the government position that our fortunes rise and fall predicated upon the United States is the Minister of State for Small Businesses and Tourism, who denies the statement. As I said earlier, he indicated that even if the United States recovers, he doubts whether we in Canada shall.
Of course, the government will try to detach itself from responsibility for the disastrous state of the Canadian economy today and from the effect it is having on small business. There are clear measures which the government could take to alleviate at least some of the hardships-and I do not mean that it should send key ministers to Houston and Paris respectively. It could scrap the National Energy Program. It could withdraw the budget. It could call an election if it really wanted to get things turned around in a hurry.
A leading businessman in Peterborough wrote to me in the wake of the budget of last November and said, with what I can only call remarkable clarity, that if something was not done soon, the country would be in a depression. Also I am sad to report that the vice-president of Silverwood Dairies in Canada said that the government should be made aware this afternoon in this debate that "the nation is not in a recession, it is in a depression".
It is clear, as it should be clear to anyone who has contemplated the major economic statistics which I cited before, that the government's plan to beat inflation through a high interest rate policy and to sustain it with consequent record unemployment is simply not working. What will it take for this government to realize that its present economic policies are not working? Obviously, this punitive budget must go. A budget which encourages entrepreneurial expansion, the creation of a savings and investment capital pool and, yes, even contemplates tax reduction, is what is needed.
A responsible Canadian government would provide tax incentives to invest or expand. A responsible Canadian government would take steps to increase the cash flow to small business through a truly revamped tax policy review. A responsible Canadian government would not insist on an addlebrained Canadian content requirement in the industrial energy sector as a condition for business activity. This is all very well on the airwaves, but the fact is that it is costing Canadians jobs everywhere and not just in Fort McMurray.
A responsible Canadian government would not force businesses to retool for international metric systems at tremendous cost at a time when small businessmen can barely meet their payroll, much less spend thousands of dollars for new scales, new tool-sets and new equipment of one kind or another- especially when the equipment they have now is good for another ten, 20 or 30 years.
To those who say that we have to go metric in order to increase and protect our export trade, I say "rubbish". The Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce and Minister of Regional Economic Expansion (Mr. Gray) will confirm, for example, a multimillion dollar deal signed last week between Vellan Incorporated of Montreal and a Hungarian nuclear plant to supply a Hungarian-built, Russian-designed nuclear power plant with 10-inch valves. This is only one of many export contracts closed in the past year which supply imperial or Canadian parts and services.
This $4 billion cost to the Canadian economy of going metric is another program for which this government should be held accountable. At last, a growing number of people are demanding the answers.
The principal question being asked is, "Why is the Canadian government trying to ruin me? Why is it making me a bankruptcy statistic in my own country?" The answer is that this government is bankrupt itself. It is bankrupt of ideas, bankrupt of principles, bankrupt of responsibility and, as we shall see in the next election, bankrupt of votes.

May 11, 1982
[ Translation]

The House resumed consideration of the motion of Mr. Speyer:
That this House, alarmed by the fact that over 1,500,000 Canadians are unemployed and aware that small businesses generate more than 60 per cent of all new jobs created in Canada, condemns this government for its ruinous economic policies, particularly those contained in the budget, which have effectively destroyed the spirit of entrepreneurship in the small business community, have contributed substantially to the loss of job-creating opportunities and which have drastically diminished investment in Canada.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-EFFECT OF ECONOMIC POLICIES ON SMALL BUSINESSES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is with great pleasure that I take part in this debate on the motion presented by the opposition, in which three points are raised. The motion accuses us of destroying the spirit of entrepreneurship in the small business community, of contributing to the loss of job-creating opportunities and also states there has been a drastic reduction in investment in Canada. Mr. Speaker, I intend to respond to the three main allegations made in the opposition motion.
To begin with, on the subject of destroying the spirit of entrepreneurship, 1 believe my hon. colleagues have often mentioned the issue of Canada's high interest rates. I think it is too easy to work on people's emotions, and certainly no one on this side of the House will deny that interest rates are much higher than we would like them to be. However, it would be very simplistic to say that tomorrow morning we are going to reduce interest rates unilaterally to around 10 per cent, without causing undue disruption of the Canadian economy. In fact, Mr. Speaker, when one of the OECD countries, namely France, decided to maintain interest rates at a level generally acceptable to the French people, this artificial measure resulted in a very substantial drop in the value of the French franc, to the point that the same government decided to bring interest rates up with lightning speed to their present level of 20 per cent. May I remind my hon. colleagues that the present prime rate in Canada is set at approximately 15.39, and that there is continued progress from week to week. However, there is no magic formula, although our hon. colleagues seem to think there is, to make interest rates drop overnight to around 10 per cent, that is, to a level generally acceptable in our economic system, although not to the prevailing levels of a few years ago.
Mr. Speaker, I am convinced that the members of this House have a duty to take the present situation seriously. However, there is a difference between what the government on this side of the House is doing and making emotionally charged speeches or causing panic among investors. In any case, last week, I met a group of some twenty-five businessmen from my riding, with an annual turnover varying from $500,000 to $25 million. They graciously agreed to spend more
Supply
than three hours of their time at a round-table discussion with the member for Montreal-Mercier to analyse the economic situation. And as the minister said earlier, I say that these people are far more reasonable, take a far more serious attitude to the issue, and are willing to co-operate in applying the corrective measures our economy needs. They realize that our economy does not stand alone and that the problems cannot all be blamed on the Canadian government. In fact, they believe that it is of vital importance to maintain the federal government's present policy and to maintain a monetary policy that will prevent the Canadian dollar from sliding downwards, which would be the case if tomorrow morning the reins on our monetary policy were loosened, and also, of course, if interest rates were allowed to drop which again would result in a drop in the value of the Canadian dollar.
Mr. Speaker, these businessmen do not believe in magic cure-alls or panaceas. They believe in difficult solutions that may be painful for some businesses, but they do not feel it is up to the government to intervene in all areas and at all times, to cure society of a disease which I do not think is caused by the government alone, but by every member of that society. The businessmen in question acknowledged that they were partly responsible for the problem and that all citizens, all consumers were partly responsible, and that, in fact, our entire society must share the responsibility. We have known prosperous and happy times, and these may well come back again, if the right measures are taken to deal with the present situation. Mr. Speaker, these businessmen are aware of the fact that there is not much room to manoeuvre, and they are willing to make every effort to get through the present situation. They did not ask me to double or reduce or be very generous and change the Small Business Development Bond program, in the belief that this would solve all our economic problems overnight. I do not think they believe in band-aid solutions. They feel that the present programs are flexible enough to enable small- and medium-size businesses to cope with these difficult times, and some went so far as to say that the present situation would weed out the weaker elements. Mr. Speaker, I trust that we shall all have learned a valuable lesson in this difficult period, and that the measures to be taken by our government, especially those announced in the budget, will enable us to overcome our problems in the not too distant future.
In their motion, my hon. colleagues refer to the loss of job-creating opportunities. Still within the context 1 mentioned earlier, namely, that the government should not take up the entire slack through unilateral measures, the fact remains that the business sector realizes that unemployment is particularly acute in two sectors, namely in the construction and forestry industries, and feels that the measures taken by this government are likely to be of some help. I am thinking of the Canada Rental Supply plan, a measure included in the budget

May 11, 1982
Supply
and passed by the Elouse which provides for the creation of some 60,000 direct and indirect jobs and has increased by some 30,000 units the supply of rental accommodation in Canada. Another program announced by the department last week and which is particularly interesting for constituencies like mine where a fair number of houses are rather old, is the Canada home renovation program. This program will help create some 10,000 jobs. In view of its flexibility, I urge my colleagues opposite to let their constituents know about it, because ultimately that measure could be beneficial to all Canadians. It is of course, people with an average salary of $30,000 per year who will be able to take full advantage of this renovation program.
However, from a description of this program, it is surprising to find how flexible it is. Among the work that can be carried out under the program, let us mention the construction of a greenhouse or such facilities; the landscaping of a permanent house; the construction or repair of fences; the construction or repair of a side entrance; the installation of various domestic appliances. Indeed, Mr. Speaker, the renovation program will enable many households to hire construction workers and take advantage of job-creation measures recently taken by this government. Another very popular program, Mr. Speaker, which now applies to houses built up to 1970, is the Canadian Home Insulation Program. This program is designed to help people involved in the building industry, people who are having problems at the present time because of the slowdown in the residential construction industry. These people will be able to benefit from an additional $280 million to complete home insulation. I believe that this program is doubly beneficial as it will help reduce energy costs on the one hand and stimulate an industry in distress on the other hand.
Mr. Speaker, when we speak about industries that are in distress, we realize that one of the most tragic aspects of the unemployment problem-and I have here the figures made public by Statistics Canada for the month of March-is of course the fact that one specific group is hit harder than the others, namely young people aged between 15 and 24, who have an unemployment rate of about 20 per cent. It is tragic to see that our young people joining the labour market cannot find any employment to test their talents, their abilities and their imagination. However, I would like to point out that our government has allocated quite recently $280 million for training and job-creation programs aimed at our young people. This is not enough to create jobs for all the young unemployed, but the private sector has certainly a significant role to play in this regard. It is obviously the private sector which should do the most.
However, Mr. Speaker, I believe that this summer the employers will have to realize that they have to take an active part in the employment programs for young people and give a helping hand to those who will be going back to school in
September. In this regard, we are providing employment offices for young Canadians which are now open to young people throughout Canada, and I hope that employers in the private sector will make use of the services offered by these offices so that our young people may work in very flexible conditions and not necessarily as permanent employees. I believe that many jobs can be done at very competitive prices and that our young people will be all too happy to contribute their talents in doing light repair work and various odd jobs that come up during the summertime.
With respect to the decrease in investments in Canada, Mr. Speaker-despite the fact my hon. colleagues do not seem to have much confidence in these data they have not as yet challenged them-I believe I can still use the budget paper entitled "The Current Economic Situation and Prospects for the Canadian Economy for the Short and Medium Term". When discussing investments I feel one must use some data, and we have those provided by OECD. I am sure we can rely on statistics produced by an organization of such outstanding prestige. We see that from 1974 to 1979, investments grew faster in Canada than in any other of the OECD countries, Canada being the only country to devote an increased share of output to investment. Thus, in recent years, Canada has shown a relatively better investment performance that any other country.
That, I feel, must be recognized and noted. In discussing investments, a distinction must be made between residential and non-residential investments, the latter being mostly that of the manufacturing or natural resources sectors. In that connection, Mr. Speaker, though hon. members opposite were quite cynical last week when the Alsands project was discussed, they should know that when it comes to viability, to investment yields, the projects involved should bear within themselves the possibility of a reasonable return. In that case, public money was involved, tax money collected from the Canadian taxpayers, and I think that the Canadian government has shown its wisdom in these rather unfavourable conditions. On the other hand, hon. members opposite did not dwell yesterday on the $600 million which the Canadian government is going to invest with Esso Resources for exploration in the Beaufort Sea and especially the implementation of our national energy policy. There is an area where investments will pay off, where the combination of private enterprise and government undertaking holds the promise of a very rewarding future, and where one of the first steps in the implementation of the Canadian energy policy can be the reconciliation of the economic interest of Canadians and the know-how of foreign companies.
My colleague who reported an increase in investment money in the United States claimed that all the investment money in Canada was leaving this country for the United States. I should like to remind him that the unemployment picture in the United States is not much brighter than it is in Canada,
May 11, 1982

and that the investment money, which is not coming into Canada is certainly not flowing into the United States. There is now a decrease in investment money in all OECD countries, as amply demonstrated by statistical data. I hope that this situation is only temporary and that the finance ministers currently taking part in OECD meetings will find ways to help our Western economies recover without disastrous repercussions on society as a whole.
My colleague, the hon. member responsible for small businesses, felt that we had better come up with solutions instead of lamenting over our predicament. Ele was right. One of the solutions which I personally favour is better co-operation among employers, employees and governments, including provincial governments, in the future economic direction of Canada. As a matter of fact, those who know something about the techniques used in Germany to plan the long-term economic future of that country are aware that the social partners sit down and discuss their economic future. I think it is high time our federal and provincial governments sat down and discussed our future with Canadian employers and employees. Recently the Minister of Finance visited many parts of Canada to meet various groups, but I think there is only one way to go about this, and it is to sit down together at the same table and talk. It is my view that a country like Canada cannot afford to waste its energies in virtually creating conflicts that should not exist with respect to this country's economic future.
Our country is mature enough for Canadian men and women to be more readily involved in the development of their economy and in the management of their businesses by ensuring that at the boardroom level employers and employees sit side by side in an effort to plan the economic future of their undertakings, to discuss productivity and quality of life at work. I believe that whatever examples we find in European countries could be very usefully followed here. Also, Mr. Speaker, I think that another avenue for concertation would be the opportunity for the employers to share their profits with the employees, when, of course, there are profits to be shared, by ensuring over-all involvement not only in management but also in equity, and in the small business sector, such a system is long overdue. Unfortunately, on account of the current recession and because of financial difficulties, management is now inviting employees to sit in their boardrooms. Mr. Speaker, I will point out that the very same employees should also be sitting at the table in times of prosperity, to plan the future of businesses. In this way we could perhaps prevent unnecessary plant shutdowns and might rapidly come up with solutions and arrive at better planning and productivity schemes. I would therefore invite my colleagues to reflect on these proposals. I share the view that small businesses in Canada may still look forward to a healthy future. We have specific programs for assisting them. We have a fiscal structure that is favourable to them, and I believe that by consultation and united efforts, the government, small businesses and labour will find ways to improve the economic future of Canadian men and women.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-EFFECT OF ECONOMIC POLICIES ON SMALL BUSINESSES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the issue we are debating today is one of the most important to be before this House of Commons for some time. Listening to previous speakers, I can understand their naivete as well as the lack of understanding of the previous speaker, the hon. member for Montreal-Mercier (Mrs. Hervieux-Payette). However, I cannot accept the ignorance, incompetence and arrogance of the Minister of State for Small Businesses and Tourism (Mr. Lapointe). His is the responsibility. I see him smirking at a time when we are trying to bring to the attention of this government the problems that small businesses are experiencing. If he would speak to some of my businessmen, the smirk would be on the other side of his face.
There are people who have spent a lifetime and have put all their earnings together only to see them go down the tube because of the policies or lack of policies of the federal government. People are brokenhearted as well as bankrupt. The place where they put their faith no longer exists.
The other day I spoke to someone working for a company which had a $10 million turnover last year and employed 100 people at any given time. Thursday night he received a call telling him to turn in his keys on Friday morning because the firm was going into bankruptcy. Yet we have the minister smirking. Canadians deserve better than that.
My colleague from Cambridge (Mr. Speyer) should be congratulated for bringing this motion before the House of Commons. As he said, from the small service companies in the petroleum industry in western Canada to the manufacturers of auto parts in Ontario to the small vessel construction in Atlantic Canada companies are in trouble.
The service companies in the petroleum industry have possibly been the hardest hit. This part of the industry was expanding more rapidly than any other segment. We tried to tell members opposite what they were doing with their National Energy Program, but they would not listen. We tried to tell them it would eventually be felt in Ontario when the service industries would no longer be able to purchase trucks and automobiles, but they would not listen.
Last January I had the privilege of travelling through southern Ontario with the task force. I came face to face with those having to deal with bankruptcies and receiverships, yet we have a minister who smirks. This is not acceptable to the people out there trying to make their way.
We must realize that the small business community provides more jobs than any other segment of our economy. At this time we have a million and a half unemployed. People are blaming the high interest rates for this. There are three components which are creating these high interest rates; it is not just the Governor of the Bank of Canada trying to protect

May 11, 1982
Supply
the Canadian dollar with high interest rates. The government has a responsibility. It has a responsibility to establish a climate in which the small business community can survive.
I agree with the hon. member for Montreal-Mercier that government should not provide subsidies to small business. It does not have to. Small business does not require that. What it requires is a climate in which it can survive. We must get away from this massive tax grab which this government embarked upon with its National Energy Program and over-all taxation policy. That is what is killing the small business community. It cannot survive. It cannot afford the expenditures of this government.
The fiscal policy of the federal government, plus the monetary policy of the Bank of Canada and the growth in our gross national product, form the basic components of our economy. Those three segments are responsible for the protection of the Canadian dollar. Governor Bouey of the Bank of Canada is trying to do all three with high interest rates. This has created the nemesis for the small business community, whether it be farming or whatever.
Based on the Revenue Canada definition of "small business", which is sales of $10,000 to $2 million, over 700,000 Canadians earn all or a yearly significant part of their income through their entrepreneurial skills as small business people. An additional 480,000 earn part-time income through businesses with sales of less than $10,000. They are the linchpin of the Canadian economy.
Small business accounts for about two thirds of our job creation. It is highly labour-intensive and has a higher ratio of jobs from investment dollars than any other segment of our economy. Small business provides more business opportunities for less skilled workers. Ninety per cent of the businesses in Canada employ less than 200 people. Small businesses account for 57 per cent of all sales in the service industry and 52 per cent of all sales in the construction industry.
As I said earlier, we in Alberta are suffering more today than in the last 50 years. A lot of our people were working in the oil service industry. Now, with the National Energy Program, with the outflow of the billions of dollars to the United States because the industry has moved south and the outflow of petroleum dollars as a result of our purchases offshore, we leave the Governor of the Bank of Canada trying to protect that amount of money, trying to protect the value of the Canadian dollar, with high interest rates and with the government reneging on its total responsibility.
We have tried to explain to the members opposite what they have been doing wrong, but they have not been listening and they will not listen, and there is as yet no sign that they are changing their attitude.
There are over 1.2 million small businesses in Canada. There are a lot of small businesses which are not trying to be small businesses. They are small because of the inhibiting influence of federal government policies. They are kept small because of the stifling and suffocating impact of the federal
government's dismal performance in the areas of economic stimulation and incentives.
Our record in research and development is one of the most pitiful in all of the industrialized world. The minister said earlier that he wished we would tell him and his government how to go about correcting the problems. Now he is not even in the House to listen. When this government opposite entered office in 1968, we were allocating about 1.5 per cent of our GNP to research and development. Now the figure is down to below 1 per cent and has been at that level for about ten years.
In the early 1970s the Special Senate Committee on Science Policy, the Lamontagne committee, pointed out the benefits of an enlightened science policy with the accent or emphasis on boosting spending on research and development to 2.4 per cent of GNP. Instead of doing that, what does the government opposite do? They chased the expertise and the technical ability that we have in our oil industry out of the country. You can make faces if you like, my hon. friend, but that is exactly what happened, and until you start to realize that this is what has taken place we are not going to correct the problem.
The United States are very clever. They do not take our labourers down there to work in their oil industries but they certainly are willing to take our expertise. If you talk to some of the people who are in the business, they still tell you that it takes two or three years to train these people. Of course, those are the people who have gone to the United States and to other parts of the world. This government will not heed and instead we as a country, as a people and as Canadians lumber along as exporters of our raw resources. We continue to be hewers of wood and drawers of water.
Dr. Larkin Kerwin, president of the National Research Council, said that we may be able to survive as a nation of woodcutters but if we do we will then have to be content to receive woodcutters' wages. Dr. Kerwin, in a recent speech, lamented that while Japan does so much with so little, Canada does so little with so much. Dr. Kerwin has told the government that an increase of just half a per cent in research and development spending as a percentage of GNP would create 400,000 new jobs. His research agency demonstrated in a pilot project that research and development seed money is returned to the investor manyfold. The pilot project I am referring to involved the investment of $93 million in about 500 projects with about 200 Canadian companies. NRC's monitoring of the results indicated that that small infusion of research and development capital resulted in new product sales of $1.8 billion. Every million dollars invested in research and development meant 1,500 man-years of jobs. The multiplier effect varied from project to project, but it went as high as 100 to one. The average return was $20 for every research and development dollar invested.
As a nation we have been plodding along, selling off our resources in raw form and then buying them back as finished imports. Let no one on the opposite side tell me that there is not a market there, because our deficit in manufactured products in any one given year would average out at about $20 billion.
May 11, 1982

My colleague from Scarborough East (Mr. Gilchrist) told the House some time ago that we are selling coal, steel, aluminum and other non-renewable resources for an average of 50 cents a pound and we are buying them back at over $3 a pound in the form of Datsuns and Toyotas.
This government has demonstrated in the past that it is not interested in developing a made-in-Canada research industry. Instead, it has been content to import technology at a great cost in jobs and growth in Canada. For a while, the door to the minister's office in the science and technology ministry was a revolving door. The joke in the department used to be: "If the minister calls, get his name." Science and technology was given, and still has, a very low priority by this government, even though it may be the key to our economic recovery and survival.
I took the time and trouble to do a little mathematics, a little arithmetic, on just what research and development could mean to this country. The National Research Council estimates that each million dollars invested in research and development requires 1,500 man-years of work-or 1,500 jobs are created for one year.
In 1981 our GNP was slightly more than $328 billion-and we spent about 0.9 per cent on research and development. If we had spent 1.5 per cent, we would have created at least 295,000 new jobs and probably closer to the 400,000 that Dr. Larkin Kerwin projected. If we had spent 2 per cent, we would have created more than a half a million jobs-546,000 in ballpark figures; and if we had spent 2.5 per cent, the recommendation of the Lamontagne committee, we would have created more than 786,000 new jobs. We tell the minister this but he is not even in the House to hear. And these figures, which come not only from the Conservative side of the House, are really on the conservative side.
Dr. Kerwin is on the record as projecting that with this kind of investment in research and development we could eliminate unemployment. How true, Mr. Speaker. We have the people, we have an intelligent people, we have a people willing to work, we have one and a half million unemployed, and we have the raw resources to put it all together. Yet we do not have a government to provide the climate to bring this about. The Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) is a graduate of the London School of Economics, an economist. Surely if he learned anything in his school years he could have put those three things together. You do not have to be a mathematical genius to figure out what the bottom line is, when just $93 million in seed money generates $1.8 billion in new economic activity. This is what we need, Mr. Speaker. That is an incredible return on investment.
Would an increase to 1.5 per cent-roughly an increase of $1.9 billion more-generate about 20 times as much or abom $38 billion in new product sales? Would an increase to 2 per cent-roughly a $3.6 billion increase-then generate 39 times as much or about $70 billion in new opportunities? Would an increase to 2.5 per cent-roughly a $5.2 billion increase in research and development investment-then generate 56 times as much new economic activity or more than $100 billion in
Supply
economic activity? These are the facts. They cannot be disputed.
Why, then, the foot-dragging on the part of the government? That is why I used the word I did, which is a strong word, Mr. Speaker, when I started to speak, when I spoke of the ignorance of the minister. Why does he and the government not heed the advice of the National Research Council? Why does it not pay attention to the results achieved by the National Research Council's experiment in funding research and development projects, in view of the staggering results it has shown that can be achieved?
If we invested 1.5 per cent of GNP in R and D, that would be approximately $4.9 billion; 2 per cent would be approximately $6.6 billion in total spending on research and development and 2.5 per cent would be approximately $8.2 billion.
If every dollar invested returned $20 on the average, the gross return on total R and D investment at 2.5 per cent would top $160 billion. That is about half of our present gross national product.
One of the most important categories of small business in Canada, along with the petroleum industry, is farming. It is hardest hit in the cost-price squeeze. It is hardest hit by escalations in the cost of energy and farm materials, of which energy is a major component cost. Farmers are big users of energy and must pass on these price increases as a cost of production. As a result, the price increases show up finally at the check-out counter in the supermarket.
Net farm income is expected to be down by about 15 per cent in 1982. This means that the figures that have already been given to us by the hon. member for Cambridge and by the hon. member for Peterborough (Mr. Domm) regarding bankruptcies will show an increase this year. High interest rates are squeezing the farmer in Canada. High interest rates are aggravating the cost-price squeeze and the cash flow squeeze.
I have received your sign, Mr. Speaker, so I guess my time has expired. I could go on because this is a serious matter. I hope that hon. members opposite will listen to those of us who are trying to explain the seriousness of the situation to them as it relates to the small business community, and I hope that they will understand.

speakeroldname: Mr. Norman Kelly (Parliamentary Secretary to President of the Treasury Board):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Treasury Board
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-EFFECT OF ECONOMIC POLICIES ON SMALL BUSINESSES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before rising to speak I counted the number of members in the House and I am therefore tempted to call a quorum. Given the difficulties that an interjection of that sort can create, however, I decided to forgo this pleasure that afternoon.
I should like to say, Mr. Speaker, that I agree wholeheartedly with the concluding comments of the previous speaker. The situation in Canada is indeed serious. I believe that there is no one in the House or in the country who would disagree that our economy is experiencing very great difficulty. If there is anyone who would argue otherwise, it must be someone who

May 11, 1982
Supply
does not have the eyes to perceive reality, the brain to understand it or the heart to respond to it.
In this debate it is important for us to realize that these difficulties are not peculiar to Canada. These difficulties, if not worldwide, are at least shared by most of the industrialized countries of the world. For we are living in a period of readjustment, one of those swing eras of the type we studied in the classroom of our youth; and we know that, in such periods, governments and peoples are forced to make choices. These will not be easy choices; they will be very hard ones. In fact, in almost all the newspapers and periodicals and all the information provided by the prognosticators on radio and television, the word that is most often used to describe the choice is "tough".
The federal and the provincial governments, then, will have to make some very tough choices in the next few years. I regret to say that, so far in the national debate on the economy by politicians, special interest and lobby groups, we have not been able to get past the rhetorical stage. That is unfortunate because rhetoric does not solve the problem; it does not point out the tough choices that have to be made; it does not indicate the degree to which we have to make sacrifices today in order to reap the rewards of the future.
There is, as well, an unfortunate preoccupation with the past in this debate. Every time a member of the opposition speaks he talks about the past-the past performance of the government or the past performance of the economy. 1 would not deny the right to that perspective but the point I make is that it is not conducive to finding solutions to our problems. In short, we have an unwarranted preoccupation with the past when we should be concerned about the future.
All too often we cast the debate in terms of personalities- whether we are for or against the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) or whether we hate him or love him. What does that give us?
Finally, the rhetoric in this debate is characterized by wildly exaggerated and vague promises of one policy or another. Very little is focused and precise in the debate. That is what is so offensive about our national debate-it is vague and deliberately so, because politicians know that the decisions to be made will be tough ones and perhaps politically damaging. As a result, they like to stay away from clearly defined or clearly presented choices. It is always nice to couch arguments in a generalized fashion so that if things do not work out, no one can criticize you for being wrong.
Mr. Speaker, I should like to move the debate beyond the rhetorical stage. I do not want to talk about the past, I do not want to talk about personalities and I do not want to talk in a vague, general way about promises. In the peculiar naivete and innocence that only a backbencher can bring to a debate at times, I should like to suggest, as clearly as I can, the choices that the government should make in the months ahead.
Before doing so, I should like to preface my remarks by saying that these choices are not necessarily those of the management, they are not final and are subject to revision without prior notice.
The goals to which all of us want to move the Canadian economy, Mr. Speaker, are obvious. We want drastically reduced inflation, higher productivity, and far higher employment levels. However, we all have to realize that we will not achieve those goals if we do not collectively-governments, corporations and citizens-lower our demands on the system and concentrate on rebuilding that system. As I said earlier, all of us, in some fashion or other, will have to deny ourselves the pleasures of the present in anticipation of enjoying the rewards of the future. This will prove a very difficult task because there are very few among us who want to forgo the lifestyle we learned to enjoy through the flush years of the 1960s and 1970s. But I would argue that we must do it, and do it now. The sooner the better.
I think everyone in this room is familiar with the television ad for automotive filters where the service repairman leans into the camera and says, "You can pay me now or you can pay me later." I suggest that is the option which faces this government and the Canadian people; we either pay the price now or we pay it later. And I am suggesting we had better pay it now because the price for solving our inflation, unemployment and productivity problems, although steep, will be cheaper now than in the future.
Let me look at inflation and suggest ways in which this government can fight inflation in the immediate future, Mr. Speaker. First of all I suggest that this government should implement a freeze to cover all wages, salaries-and dividends, because no one should escape the cold. I would suggest the freeze should last for a minimum of six months. Second, in order to make it psychologically acceptable, or at least more palatable, I suggest the government should simultaneously roll back the salaries of Members of Parliament by an amount equivalent to the present inflation rate.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not wish to be contentious, but I would prefer the hon. member to delay his question until the end of my remarks. I have a lot to say and I would like to plow through as quickly as I can in order to cover the important subject which is before the House.
I was talking about rolling back hon. members' salaries equivalent to the present inflation rate. I would introduce a slight wrinkle to that rollback, Mr. Speaker. I suggest the money saved in that rollback should be paid back to members of the House at the rate of 1 percentage point for every 1 per cent drop in the inflation rate next year. As a result, members would have a very real and important stake in fighting inflation.
Third, after the freeze is lifted, the government should introduce guidelines which would eliminate the foreign sources of inflation. If inflation is 10 per cent, employees go to their employer and ask for at least a 10 per cent increase to keep up with inflation. However, studies indicate that roughly 40 per
May 11, 1982

cent of inflation is imported from abroad. While we may have some commitment to keep people as close to the increase of domestic inflation as possible, 1 do not think this or any government, or any employer, has an obligation to compensate for foreign inflation. There is only one way to eliminate foreign inflation, Mr. Speaker, and that is to become more productive. If we do not, if we keep placing demands on the system to compensate for the foreign portion of inflation, we will never break the inflationary spiral and we will never solve our inflationary problems.
The fourth thing I would suggest is that this government should abolish all the price support systems such as marketing boards which have been created-

speechtext: How about tariffs?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Treasury Board

speechtext:
-over the last two decades. In saying that, Mr. Speaker, I do not want to suggest that I am abandoning the groups in our society for whom these price support systems were created. What I suggest we do for those people is to replace the price support systems with an income support system. I believe that if we can find the will, if we can exercise our judgment, the abolition of price support systems has the potential of decreasing inflation in this country by at least 2 per cent. That would make a valuable contribution to this war on inflation which everyone wants us to fight but for which no one wants to volunteer.
Fifth, Mr. Speaker, I would suggest a removal of all sales taxes. I have always found it passing strange that while all governments perceive inflation as the number one problem, they rarely perceive the role they have had in creating and sustaining that inflation. If you look at the prices that you pay for consumer goods today, the most remarkable thing about them is the degree to which government taxes form a substantial part of those prices. I would argue that any government which is serious about and committed to fighting inflation would abolish, or at least significantly reduce, the level of taxes it has imposed on the system, which in turn has resulted in the agonizingly higher prices.
Sixth, contrary to the prevailing advice I hear in the House, I would urge this government to make the dollar appreciate in value. Conventional wisdom argues that we should devalue the dollar in order to increase foreign sales. But I would argue that what we are trying to do through devaluation is to buy time, to buy our way out of an economy whose productivity is slowly but markedly slipping. We cannot afford, as we have over the last 20 years, to devalue the dollar continually and hope to buy our way out of our declining productivity. We cannot do it because we are forestalling the ultimate decision which has to be made on declining productivity. We cannot do it because devaluation also adds to inflation. For every three cent drop in the value of the dollar, you can add roughly one percentage point to the inflation rate we are all anxious to reduce if not eliminate. In other words, I would argue that, if we were really serious and committed as a government or as a nation to fighting inflation we would not devalue the dollar, in fact, you would appreciate it. I would offer as proof of my argument the
Supply
evidence of those countries which have been most successful in resisting inflation. They are the countries which, through the 1970s have appreciated their currencies. They are the countries with strong currencies, currencies that will get even stronger in the 1980s. If we are going to join those countries, join them in the strength of our economies, we must join them with a strong currency. I would urge this government to explore the possibility of going against the tide of public opinion and appreciate our dollar rather than devalue it.
In an attempt to fight inflation, and as a result of all the preceding advice I have given this House and government, I would urge that everything be done to lower interest rates. If we do the things I have suggested, I believe we will create a climate that will allow the Governor of the Bank of Canada, by himself or at our request to lower interest rates. I do not know how far those interest rates would fall, whether by two points or ten, but by doing what I have suggested, we would have the opportunity at least of lowering interest rates. Everyone in this House understands very clearly the dimensions of the potential that is available to us in Canada if we can only bring down those usuriously high interest rates that plague us so persistently today.
I would like to move on now to the second issue, that of higher productivity. The key to higher productivity is investment, and the key to investment is savings. This government, in one way or another, has to devise a system which promotes enhanced saving in the years ahead. In order to do this I believe the tax system has to be revised. It will have to be revised in a way that will create generous incentives for individuals and corporations to save money for reinvestment in those industries targeted by the task force which submitted its report to this House last year.
I have to confess that, at this point, I could not tell you with precision what those incentives should be, although I think that one of them at least should be accelerated write-offs. They are imperative because most of the opportunities that have been selected by the task force and endorsed by this government are opportunities that are unusually capital intensive. So if we are going to realize those opportunities and if we are going to build those industries, then we must make available the huge capital flows necessary to get them started and to sustain them. And there is only one way to do that; which is to revise the tax system and to raise the necessary money.

We should also create generous research and development incentives. There should be incentives that are targeted to the most productive industries. Those industries, I think, would be in the field of high technology. I use the word targeted because I do not know whether we could introduce universal incentives. I do not know whether we can afford to introduce universal incentives or whether, based on our limited resources, we should direct the incentives to those groups which we think can make the most use of that money.
In my comments about savings and investment, I have been referring to the private sector. We must not forget the fact that there is a public sector involved in savings and investment. I think this government, as well as other governments, has the opportunity in the 1980s to save money for the purpose of investment. In order to do that, I would urge this government to review all of its expenditures with an eye to cutting them, freezing them or limiting them in some fashion or another. It is obvious that we cannot go on spending the money in the future the way we have spent it in the past.
You will notice, Mr. Speaker, that I have mentioned spending money in the way we have been spending it. I am not arguing that we limit our total expenditures but, rather that we should redirect the money we do spend. We should direct it away from wasteful, redundant or irrelevant programs and put it into programs that will permit this government to help build the industrial infrastructure that will complement the investment of the private sector in the 1980s.
What this government has to do is to take the money it is spending on many of its present programs, collect it and reinvest it in the building of an infrastructure that complements the decisions freely taken in the open marketplace. However, if this government does that, it will have to accept two consequences. First, it will have to accept an increased indebtedness. Second, in order to raise some new capital to pay for that infrastructure, in order to raise money to replace the money alienated through the tax incentives that I alluded earlier and in order to replace any of the sales taxes that were lost from its withdrawal in the marketplace, this government will be faced with the very difficult task of having to raise taxes income in the future. I do not think this government or any other government can get away from that.
In concluding this part of my argument, let me repeat that the government will have to implement, and the public will have to accept, higher income taxes in the near future.
