speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, ordinarily I am happy to participate in a debate such as the one on the motion of the hon. member for Cambridge (Mr. Speyer), but in a sense I am somewhat ambivalent about the happiness of participating along with my colleagues because of the situation faced by small business people as a result of the November 12 budget and the paperwork burden of government which smothers initiative and any real creative thought. Later in my remarks I will refer to a specific case in my riding of the mandatory implementation of metric, without any voluntary or optional provision, increasing the costs of small businesses.
Quite frankly, Canada has bountiful resources which in effect are squandered by governments of the land. I am not overjoyed tonight to be speaking on this subject, which is generally the economy but is specifically focused on small businesses, because the situation they face is not the happy one it should be. I suppose we could not have a debate which better illustrates the quandary in which this nation finds itself and which relates more to the mainstreams of the land. We are not talking about the metropolitan megaprojects, the debate of which has, quite properly, consumed much of the time of the House, or about corporate infighting or corporate take-overs of one giant by another; we are talking about small business people. Quite frankly, as a layman I sit back and wonder what productive dollar is really being made when one corporate giant takes over another corporate giant while using the tax laws to do it at a minimal cost. This has been done even though in many cases the cost to the consumer has not been justified.
During this debate we are discussing the small business people, be they men or women. I will say small business person to be completely ecumenical, or non-generic, but I think most small-business men and women like to have the gender added since it seems to stimulate activity on the rural main streets of Canada. In any event, we are talking about the benefits of the small businesses on the main streets of Canada while at the same time discussing the sickness of this present economic policy which has resulted in bankruptcies, not only to small business persons but the bankruptcy of any serious government policy which was intended to address some of the problems confronting small business persons on a daily basis. This debate is meaningful if we are to confront those problems, because there are many small and big businesses across Canada which are trying to keep afloat. Coupled with this problem is the glaring lack of any meaningful government policy or program to help these businesses stay solvent. These programs are especially necessary when these small businesses are faced with these unconscionable interest rates, which, in my opinion, are one of the major factors of inflation in this country.
May 11, 1982

The political parties have stated their position on interest rates, but as far as I am concerned any government-including us if we were in power, as we should be-will not be able to come to grips with the problems of inflation if it just assumes that the inflationary cycle or the problems of small business persons will be resolved when we have interest rates of 18 per cent to 22 per cent.
When 1 was younger, those interest rates were thought to be unconscionable. Those were interest rates which were charged by high-flying loan companies or loan sharks. However these rates are now built into our economy on a daily basis, which results in a cash flow problem for business people who must constantly deal with interest rates. Unless we can resolve this problem-and not by government patchwork policies-we will never solve our crippling state of depression or recession which is afflicting this country.
If this debate focuses any attention or serves as a catalyst for action by members opposite it will have proven worthwhile for members to speak until termination of the debate at ten o'clock tonight.
If anyone thinks that small businesses comprise an insignificant part of our economy, they will be surprised to discover the collective effect they have across Canada. I am sure many members do not underestimate the impact of small business, but I was rather startled, after conducting some research into the matter, to discover that there are over 700,000 Canadians who earn a very significant part of their income through their entrepreneurial skills as small business people. This figure is based on the Revenue Canada definition of sales from $10,000 to $2 million, which is admittedly a rather wide definition. As well, 400,000 additional Canadians earn income through parttime employment from sales of less than $10,000. In total, that is over one million Canadians who earn income through small business.
It is as true about economists as it is about politicians that opinions vary depending on who you read or listen to, but I think most economists agree that small business entrepreneurs are really the linchpin of the whole Canadian economic fabric. During the many days of discussions on the oil and gas energy bills, my friend, the hon. member for Calgary Centre (Mr. Andre) described that industry, quite allegorically, as being the engine which would drive the economic future of Canada away from the depression or recession we are experiencing. I would suggest that long before oil and gas became so fundamental to the Canadian economy, it was the business person in both small and large businesses from coast to coast on the main streets who were and who are the engine of economic enterprise.
These small business people, who employ anywhere from 5 to 20 people, are also able to give jobs to young people during the summer to help them get through school. I feel extremely sorry for those students who will be coming out of school this summer only to find no opportunity, such as the opportunity I had when I was going to school, to earn extra money. I learned more during my summer employment than I learned in undergraduate university studies simply by being able to travel
Supply
and work in small businesses in different parts of the country. Students now will not be able to earn money for their next years' tuition through working in small business. Since the collapse of the larger megaprojects they will not be able to find employment there either. It is unfortunate, because when working in a small business you gain an appreciation, you develop a personal interest and you become prepared to work hard and honestly while earning an income to further your education. Those opportunities do not exist for students this summer, especially since the collapse of the megaprojects which would have provided them with income and afforded them the opportunity to travel as students did in my day. As well, students will not have a chance to earn income from working in small businesses in their home town. This is a tragedy which is causing anguish to many young people in this day and age.
I suggest that small business accounts for two thirds of job creation because it is highly labour intensive. Small business deserves special programs because it has special needs. The fundamental difficulty facing small business today is, undoubtedly, interest rates.
Why in the name of decency, when small business persons are faced with loan sharks and usurious interest rates, should small business be confronted with this government's policy on metric conversion, which was implemented without fundamental debate in the House? Why should the government, by moving from the old weights and measures to the new metric system, add to the problems of the small business person? I am not talking about the large supermarkets, which can afford to convert from imperial-that odious word-but about the small business person who already has enough burdens. Incidentally, one of the reasons we may have converted to metric is that we still used this old, historic word "imperial".
When government members do not get away from Ottawa- which is one of the most introverted and unreal cities to live in-and do not visit their ridings, they do not find out that a small business person on the main street of their constituency may be prepared to accept many things, but when problems are piled one upon the other, they begin to wonder who is really looking after their interests. Certainly the imposition of the metric system with no option is an added cost to the small business person which should not be borne by him.
I could go on speaking much longer about the November 12 budget fiasco brought in by the Minister of Finance. Mr. Bulloch, in a telegram, which I believe he sent to all members, illustrated the highlights of what that budget would do and how adversely it would affect the small business person. In other words, in terms of small business in Canada, it cannot resort to the same excuse that the government so often uses, but I guess any government in power would try it, that is, to slough it off to international influences. The small business person, the entrepreneur of Canada on the main streets of Canada, deserves some policy and programs to help all entrepreneurs in Canada. An attempt should not be made to slough off his problems offshore, to blame them on the Arabs, the

May 11, 1982
Supply
anchovies off Peru or the weather which affected the grain crop in Russia and all of the other excuses that we who have been in the House for the last few years have heard.
We should consider what Mr. Bulloch of the Canadian Federation of Independent Business said were the problems of the budget which would affect small business. Way back on November 18, just six days after the budget, he referred amongst other things, to the zeal to plug loopholes. We all know that this budget was a disguised tax deformity. The minister really said "tax reform". I am all prepared for tax reform, but let us debate tax reform so that we know what will happen. Let us not have tax deformity creeping into a budget here, as we had on November 12, and then having the minister recant, retreat and revise more than Napoleon. Napoleon would have been dizzy on the way back from Moscow if he had retreated, recanted and revised himself as much as the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) has done. Thirty-one times this minister has taken one step forward and two steps backward. MacEachen is the Scot from Cape Breton, from my province, and he sometimes does the highland fling. I do not mind his doing the highland fling by himself, but when he is doing it to the taxpayers of Canada, that is a different matter. The Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), pirouettes whenever he gets excited because of the Queen, executes pirouettes, as he did at Buckingham Palace and around Ottawa when the Queen left. He gets all excited and does his little pirouette. Well, that is fine for the Prime Minister. He has isolated status at the moment allowing him to pirouette whenever he wants and to pick up the photographs to show that he is a pretty vibrant individual. But the really interesting person who pirouettes is the Minister of Finance, by the name of MacEachen, the good Scot who has pirouetted more of a highland fling, not by himself but, rather, with the taxpayers of Canada, and the thirty-one step sambo that he has perpetrated on the Canadian public.
Bulloch, six days after the budget, said in a very restrained way, amongst other things, that this budget will close off access to the risk capital markets for new small business ventures and high growth medium-sized enterprises, which are the major source of new jobs. It will seriously inhibit instalment sales of any kind, i.e., consumer appliances or capital assets. It will restrict the cash flow for businesses facing excruciating pressures when financing capital expenditures at high interest rates. It will severely weaken the effective functioning of the marketplace by curtailing the ability of an owner to sell his business and restrict the number of potential buyers. It will increase the tax burden on investors in small corporations. It will discriminate unfairly against professionals who are unable to incorporate. It will restrict the ability of entrepreneurs to provide for their own retirement. It will massively increase professional fees for small businesses that must cope with more than 165 technical tax amendments. It will threaten estate planning for self-employed people, and it will create an intolerable administrative hassle for employers and employees taking any form of employee loan or advance.
Those are just some of the highlights, and how sad Bulloch's prophecy has come to be. The area I come from, the deep east, is well acquainted with adverse conditions, in a way. Quite frankly, plant closures and winter difficulty and hardship is not as foreign to us as it is to some of the places here in Ontario which have experienced pretty bountiful times, as have the areas of growth in the west with their oil, gas and tremendous mineral resources, areas where the expanding economy and progressive development has been tremendous. We in the deep east, having gone through ups and downs and having been exposed to difficult times, are a little more inured, but never have we seen bankruptcies increase as they have recently increased in my area, the Atlantic region. The bankruptcies in 1979, 1980 and 1981 bear testimony to the difficulty of the entrepreneur of Main Street in these provinces. The total number of bankruptcies in 1979 has gone from 1,043 to 1,457.1 gather that I cannot go into all the details, but 1 thank Your Honour for giving me a little hint that my allotted time, under the constrained rules of this debate, is almost over.
In Nova Scotia there were 607 bankruptcies in 1979. In 1980, there were 665. In 1981 there were 839. We do not even have the figures for 1982.
I want to tell a story which I hope will impress the gentlemen opposite. I will not go into all of the social concerns involved. We all know businessmen who have gone under. I hope that the hon. member, when he goes home to his riding, will meet some businessmen and small business people who have gone under. I am not saying it is all because of government, but I am saying to you, Mr. Speaker, that part of the reason is the unsurious, loan shark interest rates that this government, after five years, still pretends will solve the problem, but which have created part of the problem. There is no doubt about this, and this is how I will conclude, because I have been trying for three days to ask a question of the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Ouellet) concerning something called metric.
A blind constituent of mine came into my office this weekend, led by his wife who can see. He told me that he had been visited by the inspector from the Department of Consumer and Corporate Affairs who told him that, unless he converts his little scale in his little grocery operation in the basement of his house by the end of June, which is the cut-off date for that area of Nova Scotia, not only will he be fined "X" hundred dollars for every day past the deadline for conversion, but that he will also, in time, be sent to jail. This is a true story. I am trying to get the eye of the Speaker to ask the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs, without arguing the whole issue of metric, why, in the name of compassion and common sense, there can not be some exceptions and some flexibility to a program unilaterally imposed on all Canadians shown to a blind man. This man has never been on social welfare. He was not born blind, and he has lived through some tragic accidents. He is a father of three children who help him in the little store. I cannot even dignify the store by calling it a corner grocery store; it is a store on a hill in a rural part of my area, and the people there do not care whether measurements are imperial or
May II, 1982

metric. They believe in this individual. He just does not have the income to make that $3,000 conversion on his little scale from the carrots he grows and sells, for the potatoes he grows and sells and for the apples he grows and sells. He has not been a charge on the public purse in his life, and he told me very adamantly this weekend, "Patrick, if there is not some exception for a little"-I will not tell hon. members the word he used for his own operation, but one can imagine. It was a cellar operation. I was in the store. I drove 40 miles back in the hills to take a look at it. I could not believe it. It is not right for him to be told that by some inspector from Halifax, implementing a policy which we could not debate and which we do not have time to debate tonight. There must surely be some exception to this universal blanket.
Mr. Speaker, you have been kind, and I cannot continue now, but it was interesting today. Today the HUDAC people were in town. Again, to refer to small businesses and businesses which are going under in my area, businesses which are involved in the housing program and in the lumber trade, they involve McMasters and Sons and McCulloch Building Products, these are fine, established firms which have gone under. Why? It comes back to that refrain of interest rates. I hope that when the Minister of Finance comes back from Paris, he will come together with officials of the Treasury Board. Perhaps members of the Liberal caucus will go home to their ridings on the weekend, like the opposition "cauci" do, to meet their constituents. I say "cauci" advisedly, but it is a plural of the word caucus. Unless hon. members get away from Ottawa, and go back to the Main Streets from whence they came, they will not fully appreciate that there is a really serious economic problem out there which is affecting the entrepreneurs of this country. I hope the debate will stimulate a little action in a much needed area.

speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-EFFECT OF ECONOMIC POLICIES ON SMALL BUSINESSES
speechtext:

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is certainly a privilege to be able to speak on the motion presented by the hon. member for Cambridge (Mr. Speyer). I
have listened with interest to many of the speeches today. I was quite impressed with the speech of the hon. member for Scarborough Centre (Mr. Kelly) who spoke before dinner. I hope a good many of his Liberal colleagues will pay attention to his remarks, some of which will probably not be popular with them. In fact, one of his remarks will not be too popular on either side of the House.
The issue before us today deals with the plight of the Canadian business community, in particular small business. The word "small" is accurate but is very misleading at times. Taken individually, each business may be considered to be small, but as a group and through the impact of this group on the economy, the more appropriate word would be "large".
Let us consider these facts for a moment. Slightly more than 90 per cent of all businesses in Canada can be classed as small businesses. Firms with fewer than 100 employees and under $5 million in annual sales account for more than $40 billion in the Canadian economy and for 20 per cent of the gross national product. Small business employs 42 per cent of the private sector work force in Canada, or nearly nine million people. Small business contributes one third of the commercial and industrial output of our economy. Nearly 60 per cent of all new jobs created in the country this year were created by small business. Small in this instance is obviously large.
The problems being faced by small businesses in Canada today are equally large. According to figures issued by the Department of Consumer and Corporate Affairs, last year business bankruptcies in Canada rose by 22 per cent. Of some 8,055 tabulated bankruptcies, the majority were small businesses. This total does not include Firms that went into receivership or those failures where the owners just sold out their equity and closed shop.
There is an instance in my own village of Burks Falls of a business that had been established for a good number of years. It had a firm lease for ten years on the building it occupied at a reasonable rent. When the lease came up for renewal and there was obviously going to be a big increase in rent, the owner just sold the stock out and closed the doors. This excellent business location and store is now vacant. This is the sort of thing that is taking place in a great many communities across the country where the main streets now have two, or three, or sometimes more vacant premises.
A week or so ago the television news carried an item about two towns fairly close to Ottawa and showed pictures of the main streets with five or six stores closed down. That is a sizeable number in any town of 5,000 or 6,000 people.
The business community itself has set the rate of bankruptcies even higher than the figure I mentioned. Experts say that three to four times the number occur that is stated by the government. In fact, they say that last year an estimated
30,000	businesses went under. Those monitoring the activities of small business place the blame for this problem squarely on the doorstep of the government and on the government's high interest rate policy.
May 11, 1982

Some members who spoke previously mentioned the high interest rate policy of the government. A few years ago anyone charging today's interest rates would have been accused of loan sharking and would have gone to jail. 1 am well aware that a great many depositors in Canada are reaping the benefits of high interest rates, but by and large this is not good for the economy.
Small firms are almost unanimous in their contention that many of the now defunct businesses would have survived if interest rates had been lower. But the government will have no part of that argument. We have heard time and time again that the government is adamant in its belief that its policy on high interest rates is good for the nation.
A lot of good it has done the nation, Mr. Speaker. Efow good can it be for Canada when thousands of firms go belly up? How good can it be for Canada when millions of Canadians are unemployed? How good can it be for Canada when our national productivity is suffering beyond belief? How good can it be for Canada when our ability to compete in the international marketplace is put in jeopardy? Good for nothing, that is how good it is!
When large businesses get into trouble the government is quick to chase its tail in search of solutions. This inevitably means spending money, and then more money. But when small businesses tumble one by one, the government gives one of its infamous shrugs and looks the other way.
The government should realize by now that large businesses and industry depends very heavily on the small firms to supply specialized goods and services. Because of their size, small businesses can ensure quality control and the kind of detailed knowledge that is required by larger firms.
When small businesses fail, the impact is naturally felt by large business, and conversely, when large business fails or even reduces production, the effect on the smaller, support firms is obvious. When any business, large or small, ceases operations, the impact on the local and national community is horrendous.
We are all very well aware of the domino theory. A business shuts its doors and the owners and employees are out of work. These people, now having to resort to unemployment insurance benefits or social assistance, have no extra money to spend in the community. Other firms, including those that supplied the bankrupt business, soon begin to suffer set-backs and eventually have to lay off staff of their own. The cycle is predictable and deadly.
Not only does the government turn a blind eye to the situation of small business with respect to the economy, it adds to the problems in its own dealings with small business.
I see the Minister of Supply and Services (Mr. Blais) in the House tonight, Mr. Speaker, and I hope he is listening. I certainly commend his department for purchasing goods and services from small business, and I hope that trend grows. I see the minister shake his head the right way.

Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased the hon. member for Cambridge (Mr. Speyer) has chosen this topic today. It is always interesting to note that the issues of main concern to Canadians are introduced by this side of the House and very seldom, if ever, from the opposite on the government side of the House. Therefore, I appreciate the opportunity which the hon. member for Cambridge has given to us so that we can speak about a very important sector of Canada, a sector of our economy that is absolutely crucial. The hon. member identified that the small business community of Canada is taking a particularly hard beating these days. Who are these small business persons? What is this small business community to which the hon. member from Cambridge refers? Of course, the small business community of
May 11, 1982

Canada refers to something like 940,000 small firms employing one, two, three and even up to 15 and more individuals, which represents about 42 per cent of the work force which is virtually Canadian-owned and controlled. They are comprised of the small shop down the street, the independent restauran-teur, the small manufacturing shop, the individual contractor, the little welding shop at the corner and the little pop store down the street. The people who run these businesses are our neighbours and our friends. They are the people who support the Boy Scouts, the Little League, the local artistic and theatre groups, the local symphonies and so on. These are the people who have a commitment to the community and to the country. They are the people who are providing 60 per cent of all the new jobs created in Canada, both in the good years and in the bad years. The large multinationals and the branch plants do not produce jobs like the small business Canadian-owned sector does. Research and development takes place in the Small-business sector. That is where creativity takes place in this country, and where research and development goes on into new areas, new products, and new types of marketing. By and large, the small business community is the mainstream of Canada. They are the people you see when you drive down the streets of large and small communities in urban and in rural areas. They are the people I like to refer to as the builders, or the present day frontiersmen. They are the people who are prepared to move out into new areas and to take risks and chances. Some people refer to this group as the entrepreneurial group. They are the ones with ideas who are prepared to risk their life savings, prepared to toil long hours to try a new idea, to try a new way of life, and to try to build and add to the Canadian economy.
What is happening to this group within our society today, the group I suspect that all of us know very well? 1 am sure there is not a person in Canada today that at one time or another has not looked forward to being a small business person or who has not dreamed about being a small business person. The small business persons are the fabric of Canadian society. They are the basis of the Canadian economy. What is happening to these people today? What is happening to this fabric of our economic society?
Primarily as a result of the policies of the government, two million Canadians are not working today. People are not purchasing many goods and services from the small business community. Full employment is the best thing that could happen to the small business community. Full employment allows everyone to purchase goods and services. It enables people to pay the prices which the small entrepreneur requires for his or her product or service. The best thing that could happen in this country for the small business sector is full and total employment, not having 2 million people unemployed, a figure that is growing daily.
Of course, the critical blow to the small business community is the punishing interest rates which this government has now perpetuated for seven years. In an effort to combat the other enemy of the small entrepreneur, and I am speaking about inflation, the government says, "Be patient because the high

interest rate policy, given time, will result in a reduced inflation rate." But the question I must ask is, how long must we wait? This program was introduced in 1975. That was seven years ago. The inflation rate today is as high as it was when it was introduced. Interest rates have literally killed small businesses across the country.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-EFFECT OF ECONOMIC POLICIES ON SMALL BUSINESSES
speechtext:
We talk about some of the things that are happening to the small business sector. They are not very pleasant. I suppose the most difficult thing that has happened today is the fact that the small business sector is losing faith and confidence.
When you look at the 30 per cent increase in bankruptcies in the first quarter of 1982, that is 37 per cent over last year, which had an exceptionally high number. Therefore, we are talking about thousands of individuals who have experienced the pain of bankruptcy. For every person who experiences bankruptcy-and I am talking now about the first part of this year, which amounted to 3,651-there are many, many more who have experienced the agony of the receivership procedure, let alone thousands of small businessmen who have simply closed their doors and walked away from their dream, their vision of a future for themselves, their family and loved ones.

May 11, 1982
Supply
This government has literally strangled the life out of the small business sector. It has dashed the hopes and the dreams and the future of these small business people. That is the kind of reason that encourages the government to send out pamphlets, trying to convince people that all is well.
The decay of the small business sector is occurring more rapidly each day. Who stands up for the small business sector? The New Democratic Party has had its members up on their feet as often as possible in this House and in committee trying to convince the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) and the Minister of State for Small Businesses and Tourism (Mr. Lapointe) that changes must be introduced quickly. I admit the Progressive Conservatives have risen in their places to speak out on behalf of small business as well. The Canadian Federation of Independent Business has done whatever it could to lobby against the insanity of the November 12 budget and the monetary policy of this government. The Canadian organization of small business has raised its voice in hearings across the country and at every opportunity in front of the Minister of Finance. The association of business and professional people of Canada has spoken out for its membership. That association has said "Abandon the budget, Mr. MacEachen. Abandon the budget before the small business sector in this country is essentially eliminated." I will have more to say about that in a moment.
But I think it is fair to ask what can be done. Often we are criticized on this side of the House for simply trotting out a list of problems and disappointments and concerns we have, without offering solutions. Let me suggest a number of solutions that would assist the small business community.
First, the government should introduce a program that will result in a reduced interest rate for a Canadian borrower. There is no recovery program that can be introduced that is worth anything in terms of any economic recovery without a reduction in those particular interest rates. I hope that when the Minister of Finance returns from his discussions with his colleagues in Europe he will have news for us. Also I hope he will have admitted that inflation is being fuelled by high interest rates and that the way to fight inflation is first to begin a process of reducing those rates.
The need for working capital is something of which the Minister of State for Small Businesses and Tourism is well aware is a difficulty. I encourage him to work with his colleagues to introduce changes to the Small Businesses Loans Act which would provide an opportunity for working capital, particularly in critical sectors that the Government of Canada could identify for support. I beg the Minister of State for Small Businesses to lobby his cabinet colleagues to bring the development component back into the Small Business Development Bond.
This was a tragedy which the Minister of Finance laid upon the small business community of Canada when he took development out of the small business bond and said, "Here is a welfare program for small businesses." When the development aspect of that particular program was removed, the
dreams and hopes of many small business people was also removed. The government should put development back into the small business bond.
Where is the small business financing review? We have now waited about two years. The minister of state has promised that it was about to come with recommendations on how to improve the situation for small businesses in the country. Again I urge the Minister of State for Small Businesses to provide the small business community of Canada with that review so that it will see what are some of the alternatives. I hope he asks for input from the small business community as soon as it is made public.
Also I ask the minister to co-operate with the Minister of Finance and to meet with the chartered banks of Canada so that they can do what they say they would like to do with the small business bond. This was to be a program to assist needy businesses and needy farmers. All of us as parliamentarians know that small business and farmers are simply unable to take advantage of the program. The banks are refusing to cooperate, with perhaps one exception of all banks operating in Canada. The ministers must approach those banks and say that it is mandatory for them to co-operate on this particular program.
Also I ask the minister to consider altering the Small Businesses Loans Act to provide emergency short-term borrowing opportunities for businesses having difficulty. There are some real emergencies out there. When we talk about thousands of bankruptcies in the first part of this year, let alone receiverships and closed businesses, there are some emergencies which must be dealt with quickly. I suspect the Minister of State for Small Businesses will be appearing before the House shortly, asking for an extension of the Small Businesses Loans Act for at least another year. Let us look at an amendment to that particular act to provide emergency capital for the small business sector.
What about the procurement policies of government? We are r.ot holding our breath any longer waiting for the megaprojects, but there are projects which are proceeding. Let us have effective procurement policies, which will assist the small business sector. The existing procurement policies do not necessarily assist the small business sector or Canadian manufacturers but often provide for the foreign manufacturer who has an outlet in Canada as a source into megaprojects. Of course this is something the government could change very quickly.
Let us reform the Federal Business Development Bank. One thing which puzzles the small business community is what assistance is available in this area and that area, if any. Of course, small business people are often shunted from one department to another, from one sector to another. It is very difficult for the small business person who is out there struggling from dawn until dusk to make a few dollars to try to keep his business going. He does not have days on end to spend running around from government department to government department trying to find out what programs are available.
May 11, 1982

Therefore, the government should consider remodelling the Federal Business Development Bank to make it more sensitive to the needs of the small business community and perhaps to act as a clearing house for at least all federal government programs, if not federal, provincial and local government programs. It could be sort of a one-stop shopping centre for small business people looking for programs which might be able to assist them.

speechtext:
There is need for more venture capital. These are difficult times, but despite the difficult economic climate in the country, individuals and firms out there are expanding and trying new ideas in the telecommunications, transportation and exploration fields. They have difficulty obtaining much-needed venture capital or high-risk capital. Of course, this is where the government could play some role in providing assistance.
We found out today when inquiring into bank profits that some of the chartered banks of Canada have a significant portion of their capital lent out to only one company. In some cases it is as high as 30 per cent, 40 per cent, 50 per cent and even 75 per cent. There are some exceptions where 100 per cent of the capital in certain banks is lent to one business. We must ask how much money is available to small businessmen, farmers and persons seeking mortgages, if 75 per cent is lent out to one particular company. It is a very serious situation, something of which the Government of Canada should take notice and take steps to limit. The Inspector General of Banks indicated a guideline of 50 per cent to only one company, whereas in the American banking system the ceiling is 10 per cent to one company. This is the kind of situation at which we must look very carefully in order to provide an opportunity for funding and financing to the small business sector of the country.
Another area in which the government could play a much greater role is assisting the small business sector in marketing its products overseas. I understand the national trading corporation is now on the backburner and is unlikely to see the light of day. Perhaps the government could use that kind of model to provide an opportunity for the small business sector to market its goods and services in new and exciting areas. It is very difficult for the small businessman in Clearwater, British Columbia or in Chase, British Columbia to attempt to open up new markets in the Pacific Rim or to attempt to open up new potential sales in another part of Canada, which might be thousands of miles away. If there is some mechanism which the government could introduce to encourage the development of new marketing opportunities, it would certainly be an appreciated gesture in the small business community.
There are many areas upon which one could elaborate as to ways and means in which the federal government could assist the small business community. It could send out a signal to the community saying that it understands the role it plays and that it appreciates its role. The government could say, "Here are
Supply
the ways in which we plan to assist and nurture you in developing and expanding your enterprises." But the government stands back and throws up every hurdle it can, trying to create an atmosphere of discouragement, disappointment, frustration and anger. This is not what the country requires. The small business community requires leadership to provide a sound and stable economy. That is the best news which the small business community could receive.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-EFFECT OF ECONOMIC POLICIES ON SMALL BUSINESSES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this is the third occasion in perhaps a week when I have had an opportunity to speak on related subjects, in each case arising out of the suggestion of the Tory opposition that the government was inadequate in all its policies and almost always pointing to the budget as the single cause. I have heard very little in terms of any real suggestions from the Tory party except to get rid of the budget.
I have talked with many small business people who are very unhappy about certain provisions in the budget. Some people worry about some provisions; other people worry about other provisions. But I do not know of any small businessman who said to me that the budget is the real problem. The small businessman who is having real trouble is not in trouble because of the budget. He is in trouble because of interest rates and the general world economy. He rates this first, and he rates second the difficulty he is having with the Canadian banking community. Only as a third cause does he come down to the budget. Basically, if the small businessman is having trouble he is not paying taxes. If we see the budget as the main problem, how can we solve it when the small businessmen say that the budget is not the centre of the problem?
When the opposition was in power for nine months, it adopted, believed in and subscribed to a notion which was put forward by the large business community, the banking community, the Chamber of Commerce and others, that high interest rates were necessary in order to reduce inflation. Monetarism was the situation we were in and we had to stay with it.
I recall asking the hon. member for St. John's West (Mr. Crosbie), who was the minister of finance at that time, why our real interest rates in Canada, that is the prime rate minus the inflation rate, was 5 per cent or 6 per cent when the American interest rate was negative. He said that we need high interest rates because our inflation rate will go up. He said that in the House. 1 have not heard anyone in this party suggest in any fashion that high interest rates must come down even though the bankers are now suggesting this. For instance, the president of the Bank of Montreal stated that two weeks ago.
I have some difficulty understanding the general theme of this debate because it seems to deal with the problem at a rather superficial level by singling out the budget as the main problem. The opposition seems to suggest that if the budget is defeated all the problems would be solved. I cannot see that as an answer.

May 11, 1982
Supply
The solution which was suggested by the NDP was that we could have lower interest rates by implementing a form of exchange control which would prevent money from leaving the country. I do not believe that is a feasible proposition.
I would like to comment on a proposal which should be carefully considered. It involves letting the dollar drop to 75 cents, which I think is essential and should be done. However, speaking in broader terms, I would like to discuss what I would perceive to be happening today. During the late sixties and particularly during the seventies we had learned to expect as almost normal an increase in growth rates in Canada by 5 per cent or 6 per cent, such as was happening in many other parts of the world. Although the growth rate was very high in that period Canadians and people in other countries of the western industrialized world accepted it as a normal occurrence. Subsequent events, such as the general energy situation with the long and short-term shortages, the cost of oil from OPEC nations and environmental problems, made this type of growth rate almost impossible, to the point that we cannot expect this growth rate to happen in the future. Now we can only expect moderate growth rate as a reasonable possibility over the next ten or 20 years.
I recall that during the mid 1960s, when I was a principal of a high school in Thunder Bay, we were experiencing a very large growth period. There were many students coming to us, which required the construction of more schools, and there was a constant demand for teachers. We were attempting to hire teachers regularly and it was a major problem to get qualified people in our schools. I remember that the school board indicated to me that it wanted to double the size of my school-which had approximately 1,200 people-in order to accommodate the students coming into the system. Even at that time I thought that small was beautiful and I strenuously objected to having my school enlarged. I attempted to convince the school board that I did not want the school to become any larger.
To my dismay, I found that the demography was such that we were very rapidly seeing a decrease in the number of students coming in. This caused me to reflect upon the situation. In 1970, the supply of pupils to high schools in Ontario suddenly dried up. The demand for teachers and the tremendous growth in the system no longer existed. We should have foreseen this possibility and dealt with it as a country, as a province, as a city and as a school. As was described in a book called "Limits to Growth", we were in a time when high schools in Ontario suddenly found that not only was there no increase in the number of students, the number had, in fact, started to diminish. Teachers were angry because they felt the state was out to get them. There were strikes and many other problems, which caused tension in the school between teachers and the community. This situation lasted from about two to four years. I came to this job in 1972, but this tension persisted until 1976. Suddenly it dawned on the teachers and others involved in the system that this was not a plot but was actually happening. The growth rate which they had grown to expect,
of a 7 per cent to 10 per cent increase in students per year, was no longer there.
I believe that the chagrin, tension and other reactions of people in my community and many other communities was totally avoidable. When I looked back at that situation I thought that I was fortunate in foreseeing the end of this demographic growth, albeit accidentally. I thought that there must be some other approach which could have been taken to alleviate the end of this growth era which would have been better than suddenly ceasing school construction or cutting teachers back when you were attempting to hire them six months previously. I figured that there was a much more sensible way to approach this problem.
I recall considering in the early 1970s such things as worksharing. For example, if we need fewer teachers, instead of firing them and cutting back we could have a certain number performing particular functions on a full-time basis and we could hire some teachers on a part-time basis and have a phase-out retirement plan at the same time.
What I was attempting to do was to understand the nature of this very massive change which occurred to the people in that community and many others. This is small part of the whole picture, but I submit that the entire problem we are facing today was predictable in 1976 when our Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) was ridiculed for suggesting that this was, in effect, what was going to happen, that there would be some very major changes in our social structures which would cause us to do many things which we would not be very happy about. There would be much chagrin and strife in our society. When the Prime Minister predicted this, he was almost booed out of the country because it was very disturbing to say that the free market system was not working.
It was unfortunate that that particular wording was used because everyone singled out that particular area. The House was in a great state of confusion because the Prime Minister has said that. We should have listened to what he said at that time because that is what is happening today. It is unfortunate that the factor which has slowed things down or has brought about much of this chagrin has been high interest rates. I can certainly sympathize with those people who saw monetarism as one approach to the problem. Of course, one of the problems of the modern era and one which we have to learn to live with is the fact that there are not simple answers and that macroeconomics do not work. It was formerly very effective in the sixties. One could say that the Keynesian theories work well. If they did not work perfectly, it was because we did not time them properly. But we can basically stimulate the economy by fiscal arrangements and some minor monetary arrangements. We can either slow it down or stimulate it. We are fairly effective at it.
As I say, the only reason we failed, or were not as effective as we could be at solving some problems, was that the timing was not right. But there was a workable system. However, these solutions are not working any more. We have stagflation,
May 11, 1982

which is a contradiction in itself, and we have the use of the monetary system which creates more problems than it is worth. All of this is going on, but I maintain that we are in a new era and those solutions just do not work. That is why I do not understand why people are so critical in saying that the government must resign if it tries something which does not work. It is because there are no simple answers. We are living in a very difficult, very fragile, strife-torn era. It is not easy to govern at this point and we will have to move in several different directions.
I am suggesting that I do not like high interest rates because they are indiscriminate. They may not affect me because I happen to have a 25-year mortgage on my house, but someone else who has a five-year mortgage may, all of a sudden, find that his interest rate has risen from, say, 10 per cent to 17 per cent, 18 per cent or 19 per cent, doubling his mortgage payments and hitting him very hard. If something else happens, for instance, if he loses his job, then he could very well lose his home because he does not have sufficient equity. Therefore, there are some very massive problems affecting people, and they are indiscriminate.
In the period between 1970 and 1976, I would have liked to have seen an easing of the school problems so that they would not turn into a complete revolution. In 1976, the Prime Minister and others were ridiculed for their views as to how to ease these problems, but these views should have been considered by others.
In the two or three minutes left to me, I very strongly suggest that we should adopt the policy being followed by the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen), which is to push very hard at the summit for some real relaxation in the U.S. interest rates. Of course, at the present time the American real interest rate is ridiculous. It is about 14 percentage points. Ours is about 6 per cent. This is one way that we must move. Certainly, what the Americans do is very important. However, I suggest the other way is to consider very seriously the study commissioned by the Financial Times and announced about three weeks ago. It requested Data Resources, Informetrica and the Conference Board to find out what would happen if the dollar were pegged all of a sudden at 75 per cent. The results were quite interesting. There were several approaches to their findings, but their basic conclusion could be summarized in the idea that somewhere along the line we would likely have a 12 per cent prime bank rate, we would likely create about 100,000 new jobs and we would likely have an increase of about 2 percentage points in inflation. I am not suggesting this is something we should do or that we should wing low if we do not have to.
We must put enough pressure on the U.S. government. When 1 refer to the U.S. government, I do not simply mean the Reagan government. I am referring to support from those other Republicans, and certainly the Democrats, who find Reaganomics to be an extremely unworkable system. I think we must put pressure on and support those people who are also moving in this direction in the United States, because the U.S. government is in very bad shape. There are some major things happening in the United States, particularly in the area of
Supply
disarmament, and it is affecting that government. It is quite possible that the government will have to reduce its defence spending for many reasons, and one of them would be to reduce its deficit. Do not forget that when the U.S. deficit of $130 billion or $140 billion is compared to our deficit on the ratio of 10 to 1, it is really about twice as drastic because the American savings rate is about half the Canadian savings rate. That makes a very large difference when considering a deficit of $140 billion. Our savings rate over the decade has run about 10 per cent or 11 per cent, while the American rate has been about 5 per cent or 6 per cent. Therefore, a $140 billion deficit, even though it is only ten times our deficit, is significantly more dangerous to the U.S. economy than to our economy.
If we are not successful in the next month or two or three, and if President Reagan and his government refuse or make no effort to lower interest rates, and if the Federal Reserve Board does not move on the situation at all, then I suggest that we must try to move independently. I do not think we can do anything with exchange controls as the two economies are too closely related. We must let the dollar drop.
I think there are other things we must consider. It seems to me that it is very important in our society today that we carefully ease into this different period to which we are moving and that we ensure that the people in our society who are most harmed by high interest rates and other problems are protected. We as a government must be more solicitous toward these people. We must find ways to ensure that people can get work.
I strongly commend the efforts of the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Axworthy) who has embarked very seriously on a program of work-sharing. When it is not possible to create the jobs that our society would like or needs then it may very well be necessary to share the work available among a much larger group of people.
I could go a long way toward discussing work-sharing because I think work-sharing has much to do with productivity. Most areas in which there is work-sharing have shown great increases in productivity because people tend to be more productive over a shorter period of time. I gave a long speech on this in 1976 or 1977. To me, the work I had done indicated that this would be a very successful approach to the entire problem. I am saying that we must do some things which are quite different from the kinds of patterns we followed in the past. I am always disappointed that the New Democratic Party is not trying to look at some of these new features which must be considered as we change from a very large-growth society to a moderate-growth society.
Therefore, in closing, I would suggest that the debate in this House might well concentrate more on the massive changes which are occurring. We must consider how the people in the country and in the world can be brought into this new era with a minimum amount of discomfort.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-EFFECT OF ECONOMIC POLICIES ON SMALL BUSINESSES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I sometimes wonder why this government has a minister responsible for small business at all because it is clear from the

May 11, 1982
Supply
actions of the government since it came back to office in 1980 that it believes in only one thing, that big is beautiful. The government operates like its mandarins do. Its mandarins understand big business because big business and big government play in the same kind of sandbox. They operate the same way. The concepts of big business are the same concepts as those of big governments. During the period 1980-1981, a disaster befell small business. Under the government's Canadian ownership program, its nationalist ownership scheme, the banks have been directed to finance massive take-overs of business through bank borrowing. Tonight 1 want to show some of the things that have happened in terms of bank borrowing which has starved small business of funds. It has caused home owners, fishermen, farmers, small business people generally to pay rates of interest described in this House tonight as totally usurious. At some point rates of interest have been 5'/z per cent above U.S. rates, rates that no business, small or large, can carry. Certainly small business, which does not have the resources of big business, has no possibility of carrying those rates of interest.

In the period since October, 1979, the end of the bank year, bank loans of over $5 million amounted to $16.9 billion. Large loans today are $39.6 billion, an increase of well over 100 per cent. What happened to relatively small loans? According to the bank statements, in October, 1979 small business loans under $1 million, which we will call relatively small loans, were $16.9 billion. After three years, with inflation running at 10 and 12 per cent, those loans now amount to $20 billion.
The banking system has been directed by the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen), who is responsible for the banking system under the Bank Act, to take over all foreign companies in the country and to finance huge movements of capital. Massive bank loans have been made to large corporations which would normally go out on the market and borrow money in the stock market. However, they have borrowed with bank financing, literally starving small business, and have bid up interest rates unconscionably. The federal government, which is responsible for banking, has allowed that to happen.
Large businesses have borrowed most of the $20 billion for Canadian businesses that Canadians now owe foreigners in foreign currency liabilities. The effect has been a disastrous run on our currency.
In order to maintain any sense of parity on the dollar, over the past year we have had to pay between 2 per cent and 5 per cent more than anybody in the United States, certainly higher interest rates than most other OECD countries.
This has been a deliberate policy, which was damaging to small business by a federal government that claims, as the minister claimed when he sent out a quarter million pamphlets on the budget to small business people, and he claims every time he sends out bumf with respect to the Federal Business Development Bank, economic development loans, grant programs and various other things he has in his quiver, to show he is there to help small business. He has been organizing the
financial affairs in this country in such a fashion as to starve small business of money and force up interest rates.
What is the purpose? It is because the mandarins like the mandarins. They like to look after their own type. Over the past two years they have used the credit system in this country to damage seriously those people who want to run a store, small factory, fish plant, trawler or a farm, those people on the main streets in Canada about whom the hon. member for Annapolis Valley-Hants (Mr. Nowlan) spoke.
We know how the system operates in favour of large corporations. There have been massive borrowings by Chrysler, Massey-Ferguson and other corporations which have got into trouble. In that kind of situation, the banks somehow all of a sudden, have a non-interest bearing loan. They come to the assistance of those companies and so does the government. Somehow, somewhere, they convert some of those loans into an equity of some kind. They do some kind of reorganization, something to protect those large loans. The government helps them. However, what does the government do for the small fellow who must close or be sold out under power of sale? What does the government do when the banker tells some people they must double their collateral, provide their wife's signature, and give a mortgage on their home or the bank will close them down? Are those loans put on hold? Are they put to the side? Are these classified as non-interest bearing loans? Are the loans negotiable? Not really. These small businessmen do not have the clout. We have a situation where the government has not taken its responsibility seriously with respect to interest rates and the way lending is carried out to ensure the total community has an opportunity with regard to the resources, savings and other things that should be available to it.
I was hoping to have more time to speak about the budget. The minister said he sent out a quarter million pamphlets saying how wonderful the budget was for small business. We know the answer, and we have known it ever since budget night, November 12.
A 12'/2 per cent tax was placed on dividends. Capital cost allowances were cut in half. A sale or exchange was a deemed sale or purchase for cash. Capital gains continued to be treated as a capital gain, even though most of the gain is inflationary. We saw what was done to the Small Business Development Bond. The program was gutted. No businessman I know of who did not already owe money to the bank has been able to take advantage of the new small business bail-out bond, the welfare bond authorized in that budget.
There has been no effort by this government since taking office to come to the aid of small business people and make capital more available, keep interest rates down and provide an incentive and an opportunity to grow and build.
This country was built on small business by people who were entrepreneurial. They went out and did things. They created. These people were imaginative. They worked 16 hours a day, seven days a week. They mortgaged their homes and borrowed from friends and relatives just to get an operation going. Many times they did not succeed. How could they succeed when the
May 11, 1982
government deliberately organized the financial affairs of the country so that they have had it?

PUBLIC WORKS-REQUEST THAT COMPETING FIRMS BE REIMBURSED FOR EXPENSES. (B) REQUEST FOR INDEPENDENT INVESTIGATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise tonight to deal with an issue which I think has unfortunately put the office of Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) of our country into a very bad light indeed. One always hopes in political life, amongst people who are interested in the welfare of our country, that our Prime Minister will occupy a position in which he will give leadership in terms of matters of integrity, in terms of the kind of actions that are illustrated throughout his government and the party that supports him in the leadership of a government and the leadership of a country.
I am sorry, therefore, Mr. Speaker, to have to rise tonight in the adjournment debate to indicate my very grave dissatisfaction with the way in which the Prime Minister has responded to some very serious questions about political patronage, about cronyism, about the awarding of contracts to friends of the Prime Minister, as opposed to following the well-established rules for tendering, which should be followed by any government worth its salt. As a result, I think it is important for us to have a quick look at some of the background of this particular situation.
Hon. members will know that the matter of the design of the Washington embassy in the United States originated by the government establishing a selection board. That selection board consisted of seven members chaired by a retired and distinguished diplomat, Mr. A. Edgar Ritchie. There were two representatives of the Royal Architectural Institute, two representatives from the Department of Public Works and two representatives from the Department of External Affairs. About 2,000 firms were canvassed with respect to submissions to be made in connection with the design of this project; and 318 architectural firms responded. In the final analysis, 71 firms put in submissions.
I should point out, Mr. Speaker, that these firms spent considerable moneys in terms of submitting these proposals, on the basis that they would be processed through the selection
Adjournment Debate
panel and that there was some legitimacy to this whole process because it had been established by the government.
The information that we have is that the 71 firms in question spent some $10,000 each on their submissions. Of the 71 firms that made submissions at some considerable expense, 11 firms were finally selected by the selection panel. These 11 included Mr. Erickson.
In November, 1981, this group was invited and in fact visited Washington to discuss the plans for the new embassy and to observe the site. They were subsequently brought back to Ottawa for a discussion with the panel at extensive and additional expense. The information we have is that the minimum expense for those last firms was somewhere between $40,000 to $60,000 each. An average of $50,000 would give a total of $550,000. That, added to the $710,000 spent by the 71 firms orginally, means there was an expenditure of over $1.25 million dollars, in terms of the firms offering themselves for this particular important project.
After considerable discussion with the final 11, the panel reduced that number to four finalists. One of the four finalists was deemed to be outstanding. Zeidler Roberts of Toronto were judged by the panel to be outstanding, the other three firms being in the running but not in the same category.
The chairman, Mr. Ritchie, has stated with respect to Mr. Erickson: "Erickson was unlikely to do as good a job as the four finalists in this case." That was his considered opinion.

speechtext:
That was on the basis of expert opinion, expert advice that was received. We find now, Mr. Speaker, that the information we have now is that Mr. Erickson in fact knew some two years ago that he was going to get this job, notwithstanding the charade with respect to the selection process.
The fact of the matter is, Mr. Speaker, that we now have a very serious situation when the Prime Minister puts out a very misleading release in respect of the appointment of Mr. Erickson, in which he suggested that the selection panel had indicated that Mr. Erickson was somehow a selection of that panel-which was quite contrary to the fact.
What the Prime Minister is telling us now is that he alone is the expert in terms of choosing architectural expertise and design and that his opinion should prevail over that of the selection panel. If he was so dissatisfied with the conclusions of the selection panel, was he saying that it was incompetent? If he was not satisfied with its recommendations, why did he not refer the matter back to the panel for further consideration? He should have done that if it was the opinion of the government that none of the four finalists really qualified.
We have a situation where the fix was in before the panel had a chance to come to a decision. The tendering process was a charade. The Prime Minister was pork-barreling. Apparently

May 11, 1982
Adjournment Debate
there are new rules and unless there are compelling reasons to the contrary, favouritism prevails.
The people of Canada will not put up with this, Mr. Speaker. They have had enough of the Prime Minister and his extravagant ways, and now he is wasting public money on political patronage. I say that the time has come for the Prime Minister to accept the proposition of an independent investigation into the conflicting statements that have been made in this matter. If he refuses, then I say that indicates that he is afraid of the findings that an independent commission might make. If he has nothing to be afraid of then he should allow an independent investigation into this matter. I thought that anyone in this country who by deceit, falsehood or other fraudulent means defrauds any person, whether ascertained or not, of any property, money, valuables or securities was guilty of an offence. I thought that was still the law in this country.
