speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council; Deputy Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party Deputy House Leader
subtopic: PUBLIC WORKS-REQUEST THAT COMPETING FIRMS BE REIMBURSED FOR EXPENSES. (B) REQUEST FOR INDEPENDENT INVESTIGATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would urge the hon. member for Saskatoon West (Mr. Hnatyshyn) to read a recent article which appeared in Fortune magazine in which architects in North America were discussed. In that article Mr. Erickson was described as the foremost architect in North America. Any suggestion that he is not eminently qualified to carry out this assignment is pure and utter nonsense.
We live in a parliamentary democracy. One of the fundamental and basic premises of a parliamentary democracy is responsible government, and that means that the incumbent prime minister and ministers are responsible for what the government does.
It may well be that officials might decide to set up a panel which, as was done in this particular instance, will assess the technical competence of architects and suggest a number, all of whom would be qualified from a technical point of view, who are eligible to do the job. That is what was done in this case.
In the final analysis, as the Prime Minister has repeated again and again in the House, he and the cabinet take responsibility for the decision that was made.
It is correct that the bureaucrats, or whatever you want to call them, said that 11 architects were competent to do the job. Mr. Erickson's firm was amongst that number although it was not ranked first. The hon. member is quite correct about that.
As the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) has said, we live in a parliamentary democracy in which the cabinet and the ministers take responsibility for the decisions they make. Mr. Erickson is the most honoured architect in Canada; in terms of awards he wins hands down. I think it is reasonable that a prestigious building on a prime location in Washington should have the best that we can produce.
Mr. Erickson has disputed the statements made in this morning's Globe and Mail. I think it is quite irresponsible for the hon. member to go off on a witch hunt based on that report.
We should all be proud that a greatly honoured architect has agreed to do this building. It was obviously a wise decision and one of which we will be proud for many years to come.

subtopic: BANKRUPTCIES-POSITION OF PURCHASERS OF INSURANCE FROM COMPANIES PLACED IN RECEIVERSHIP. (B) REQUEST THAT PURCHASERS BE TREATED AS PREFERRED CREDITORS
BANKRUPTCIES-POSITION OF PURCHASERS OF INSURANCE FROM COMPANIES PLACED IN RECEIVERSHIP. (B) REQUEST THAT PURCHASERS BE TREATED AS PREFERRED CREDITORS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, most people who hold insurance policies on their business premises, their homes, their cars and even their health and their life assume that in the event of a claim the policy will be valid, that the insurance company will be in business and that their claim will be paid.
Unfortunately, Mr. Speaker, that is not necessarily so because events over the past year reveal that insurance company failures can leave policyholders seriously exposed. In other words, policyholders who regularly pay their premiums and renew their insurance on a regular basis, who presume they are covered and expect their claim to be paid in the event one is made, are really in effect living under a false sense of security. In this context I addressed questions to the Minister of State for Finance (Mr. Bussieres) last Friday as reported at pages 17166 and 17167 of Hansard where I drew this to the attention of the minister. He indicated that he was aware of the situation and that certain actions on his part were going to take place. The reason I brought it to the attention of the minister is that I have a case which has been brought to my attention where a statement of claim has been filed and the policyholder has just been advised that because his insurance company is being liquidated there will not be sufficient funds left over to cover his claim. The insurance company involved is Pitts, and my constituent received a letter dated March 2, 1982, from the law firm of Milner & Steer. Before I quote from the letter, I would once again point out that while this is a small claim, it could be a very substantial amount. Nevertheless, the principle remains the same. Milner & Steer are solicitors for Pitts Insurance Company, and the letter says:
You may have recently heard that Pitts Insurance Company has been woundup, pursuant to a Court Order granted by the Supreme Court of Ontario at the request of the Federal Superintendent of Insurance. The Superintendent has been appointed as the Provisional Liquidator of Pitts, and the Clarkson Company Limited has been appointed to act as the agent of the Provisional Liquidator. In turn, The Clarkson Company Limited has retained the Toronto law firm of Goodman & Goodman to look after the legal aspects of the winding-up.
We have recently been advised by Goodman & Goodman that the assets of Pitts Insurance Company are insufficient to provide full coverage under the various policies of insurance. In this regard, we have been instructed to advise you that, in the event that Mr. Mapletoft's claim is successful, Pitts will not be in a position to pay 100 per cent of the claim. Accordingly, Beverly Crest Motor Inn Ltd. will be responsible for any deficiency.
That pretty well sums it up, Mr. Speaker. There are other companies which have gone bankrupt and rumours of more. The issue of solvency of insurance companies, and the effect upon the policyholder in the event of bankruptcy, is a matter
May 11, 1982

which has been raised before the appropriate standing committee. Away back in December of 1981 the minister gave essentially the same answers to the committee that he did in the House. Really, the expected corrections or changes in the legislation are not anticipated to be brought forth until the fall. Basically, what he is doing here is waiting for recommendations from the Superintendent of Insurance. Through you, Mr. Speaker, I ask the parliamentary secretary, what about the losses faced by the policyholders? They bought an insurance policy in good faith and expected their insurance company to honour any legitimate claims. Why are policyholders being asked to settle their own claims?
In a matter where two companies went bankrupt, Pitts and Strathcona, there was an agreement by the insurance companies to establish a fund in the case of Strathcona so that all unsettled claims would be paid. Surely, Mr. Speaker, the government has a responsibility here to provide the kind of climate that will preserve the integrity of the insurance company business. Surely it is inappropriate for people who in good faith buy insurance policies to have nothing more than a worthless policy when they come to make a claim. People in business buy this protection and expect to have the security. The superintendent is charged with the responsibility of monitoring. When he deems there is financial trouble, he is supposed to recommend and take the necessary corrective action. But as I said before, in the case of Strathcona, a consortium of insurance companies agreed to honour all claims. However, that is not the case with Pitts. Why is there a double standard?
The minister and the superintendent have indicated that some changes will be made, such as amendments with regard to reserve margins of capital and security, insurance treaties, tighter controls in the case of re-insurance, and the general rating of financial standards. But that will not solve the problem we face now, I believe we face two problems now. They are the losses and the confidence of the insurance industry and insurance companies. What is needed as well is to give the superintendent more than simply an advisory and a monitoring role. As it now stands, he cannot act until it is too late. He also needs broader disciplinary powers beyond fining or winding up. There is considerable doubt that the superintendent reacted quickly or firmly enough in the case of Pitts and Strathcona. In my view he needs to be mandated to assist those failing companies vigorously. Confidence and security are vital to the insurance business, and the superintendent must have the power to ensure that stability and solvency exist. As a matter or principle, I think the minister should move very quickly to implement these changes without delay so that the integrity of the insurance system can be preserved and upheld. Immediate steps should be taken to save any losses that may accrue to those policyholders who now have claims that are not being settled.

speakeroldname: Mr. Jim Peterson (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Justice and Minister of State for Social Development):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State for Social Development
subtopic: BANKRUPTCIES-POSITION OF PURCHASERS OF INSURANCE FROM COMPANIES PLACED IN RECEIVERSHIP. (B) REQUEST THAT PURCHASERS BE TREATED AS PREFERRED CREDITORS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to respond to this question. As the hon.
Adjournment Debate
member is aware, we have a very strong record in the insurance industry in Canada. In the last 50 years we have had only three federally incorporated insurance companies that have experienced this type of financial difficulty. Unfortunately, in 1981 there were two. That is three companies in 50 years so I do not want the public to think that if they go to an insurance company and put their premiums there that they are at risk in suffering grievous harm. Our insurance industry, as I shall conclude later, is on a very sound financial footing. I think our record over the years indicates this.
The fact is, as the hon. member has pointed out, we have had two failures. In the case of Strathcona, friends of the company rallied around to make sure that the people who placed their money with that company were made whole. In terms of Pitts, it has been a different matter. Pitts has not been able to meet its obligations. But the remaining assets are going to be reserved for the policyholders. As we are aware, the provisional liquidator is still in the process of investigating what type of proceeds will go to those policyholders. The preliminary indications are that they will receive a substantial sum. But it would be inappropriate for us to guarantee or undertake immediate action on this particular matter until we have all the facts in hand. I can assure the hon. member that this question is under very active investigation and we hope to realize as much from the assets as is possible.
The reasons for the failure of these two companies in the past year relates to low premiums and very healthy competition in the market-maybe excessive competition-and also a record number of claims. Nevertheless, in spite of this climate which prevailed last year and which led to the bankruptcy of these two companies the industry as a whole, because of its investment income, had a profit. This year, in order to correct this measure, the companies are increasing premiums. The superintendent is still undertaking his investigation. This investigation will continue. We are still looking for concrete ways to help resolve these problems in the future. I can assure the hon. member and I can assure Canadians that this is a matter of great concern to us and we look forward to proposals on how we can proceed in the future.

subtopic: THE JUDICIARY-STATEMENTS ON CONSTITUTION MADE BY BRITISH COLUMBIA SUPREME COURT JUSTICE. (B) JUDICIAL COUNCIL INQUIRY
THE JUDICIARY-STATEMENTS ON CONSTITUTION MADE BY BRITISH COLUMBIA SUPREME COURT JUSTICE. (B) JUDICIAL COUNCIL INQUIRY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on March 8, 1982, the Canadian Judicial Council ordered a formal investigation into certain complaints lodged by Federal Court Trial Justice George Addy about the conduct of Mr. Justice Thomas Berger, a respected judge of the British Columbia Supreme Court, a ten-year veteran of that court.
The basis of Mr. Justice Addy's complaints were certain statements which were made by Mr. Justice Berger, both in The Globe and Mail and in a speech at the University of Guelph which was subsequently reported in that journal. In those particular speeches Mr. Justice Berger was critical of the constitutional accord which had been arrived at between the provincial premiers and the first minister. Mr. Justice Addy's letter was addressed to the Judicial Council and was dated on

May 11, 1982
Adjournment Debate
November 18 and November 19. In that letter he indicated that in his view Mr. Justice Berger's conduct was, among other things, worse than sleeping with prostitutes or drunk driving.
Just a few days later the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), speaking on a television program hosted by Mr. Jack Webster, stated, "I just regard this as the judiciary getting mixed into politics and I hope the judges will do something about it". Clearly the Prime Minister was urging the Canadian Judicial Council to take action on Mr. Justice Berger's comments. Mr. Justice Berger stated, "If he had wanted to do this, I wonder why he didn't support the bill when he was there and when it gave Quebec the veto and gave the Indians aboriginal rights; he didn't support us then." As I will show very shortly, that statement is patently false.
The two issues raised by Mr. Justice Berger transcend narrow partisan politics. First, with respect to the question of aboriginal rights, it was Mr. Justice Berger's view that the constitutional accord which had been arrived at failed in the promises that had been made to aboriginal peoples. He stated in his speech at the University of Guelph in November of last year:
The agreement reached in February this year by ail parties in the House of Commons, to entrench aboriginal rights and treaty rights in the new Constitution, has been repudiated by the Prime Minister and the premiers.
He went on to give some history and to say:
There was, at the end, not one of our Canadian statesmen willing to take a stand for the rights of the Indians, the Inuit and the Metis.
At the end of the article it read:
This is not the end of the story. The native peoples have not come this far to turn back now. But it is an abject and mean-spirited chapter. No one can rejoice that it was written in Canada.
He spoke as well in opposition to the removal of the veto power for the province of Quebec. On these fundamental questions in both instances ultimately the Prime Minister agreed that a mistake had been made. There was a restoration of aboriginal rights to the constitutional resolution, albeit a qualified restoration, and the Prime Minister has said publicly on a number of occasions since the signing of that package that he would support the restoration of the veto power for the province of Quebec.
We are not dealing with a narrow political issue in the everyday partisan sense. We are dealing with a fundamental fabric of the nation, the Constitution of the nation. Who better to speak out on these questions than Mr. Justice Berger himself, the respected author of the Berger report into the Mackenzie Valley pipeline. The Prime Minister is guilty of the worst sort of hypocrisy in attacking Mr. Justice Berger on this instance when he stood silently by in 1970, for example, when Mr. Justice Freedman supported his invocation of the War Measures Act or indeed when Mr. Justice Berger himself, in September of last year, supported the constitutional resolution as it then was, with its inclusion of aboriginal rights and its respect for the veto power of the province of Quebec.
This is nothing less than a judicial witch-hunt by the 27 most senior judges in Canada. In my view they should be ashamed of themselves for taking part in this rather sordid
spectacle. It is one of the most meanspirited and shabby chapters which has been written in the judicial history of Canada for some time. This is only the second inquiry in the history of the Judicial Council. I am sorry that the Canadian Bar Association has not seen fit to speak out on this important question and indeed that Mr. Justice Berger's fellow judges have all remained silent on it. We do not intend to remain silent on this important question or on this fundamental issue. I have called upon the Prime Minister and the Minister of Justice (Mr. Chretien) to make public all documents surrounding this serious allegation and as well to use his powers under Section 40 of the Judges Act to order that the hearing of this particular matter be held in public.
The Minister of Justice can attempt to evade responsibility by saying that the Judicial Council is the master of its own affairs, but under Section 40(6):
An inquiry or investigation under this section may be held in public or in private, unless the Minister of Justice of Canada requires that it be held in public.
I strongly urge the Minister of Justice to take that step and let the people of Canada see this judicial witch-hunt for exactly what it is.
In closing, I would like to quote from Judge Irving Kaufman of the United States Court of Appeals of the second circuit, a very respected American judge who dealt with this important issue in the New York Times in an article entitled "Judges Must Speak Out". He said:
In the final analysis, when the public interest requiring that judges share their special expertise is balanced against the risk of a seeming impropriety, the scales tip heavily in favour of expressing one's views.
The public may remain confident that judges will follow the advice they give to juries: A case must be judged on its own merits, not on one's personal predilections.
He goes on further to state:
Judges have the duty to speak on matters that affect the judicial system because the public interest cannot be served by silence. Silence is not always golden.
In this case, Mr. Justice Berger was speaking out with courage on a matter of fundamental importance to Canadians, particularly to minorities. Instead of being criticized for that, he should be commended.

speakeroldname: Mr. Jim Peterson (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Justice and Minister of State for Social Development):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State for Social Development
subtopic: THE JUDICIARY-STATEMENTS ON CONSTITUTION MADE BY BRITISH COLUMBIA SUPREME COURT JUSTICE. (B) JUDICIAL COUNCIL INQUIRY
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, my colleague from the opposition already pre-judged the situation he has been referring to. The Canadian Judicial Council established by the Judges Act consists of the Chief Justice of Canada as Chairman and the Chief Justice, associate Chief Justice and Assistant Chief Justices of each Superior Court in Canada. That council may enquire into and investigate complaints or allegations made in respect of a judge. The Council decided on March 8 to investigate a complaint filed in November 1981 against Mr. Justice Thomas Berger. When the investigation is completed, the Council will
May 11, 1982

submit a report on its conclusions to the Minister of Justice (Mr. Chretien).
It is of prime importance to know that the Council consists of the most competent justices in this country and that they took the decision to act on the complaint filed against the judge. I am informed that the investigation is the first one to stem from a complaint filed by a person other than the Minister of Justice. The Council has been meeting since 1971, and receives some 30 complaints every year.
It is also very important to know that the Chief Justices who sit on the Council are fully aware of the basic principles of justice and equity that must apply in such investigations. The Judges Act sets the major guidelines pertaining to such investigations and, in addition, the Council also established rules of procedure for the holding of such investigations. In view of the foregoing, the Minister of Justice concluded it would not be appropriate to require that the investigation on Justice Berger be held in public. It would be much better for the Council, which is responsible for promoting high standards of effectiveness and uniformity in the administration of justice
Adjournment Debate
within superior and county courts, to make all the important decisions that will lead to the conclusion of this inquiry.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, it would be improper to make remarks on the subject matter of the inquiry. The Council must be allowed to deliberate without any interference whatsoever. Everything must be done to ensure that the inquiry and the findings are based entirely on essential principles of Canadian law.
